title: Logic and set theory
basics: Logic says which conclusions follow from which assumptions, and set theory (usually ZFC) gives a shared foundation in which nearly all of mathematics can be written down.
deeper: A proof is a finite chain of steps from axioms by fixed inference rules. Because the foundations are chosen by convention, some statements (like the continuum hypothesis) turn out to be independent of ZFC.
expert: ZFC: Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms + choice; |ℕ| = ℵ₀ < |ℝ| = 2^ℵ₀ (Cantor). CH independent of ZFC (Gödel 1940, Cohen 1963).
regime: Pure formal reasoning; physics uses it as a language, not as evidence.
evidence: Nearly all published mathematics can be formalised in ZFC
Independence proofs (forcing) show where ZFC is silent

title: Gödel's incompleteness theorems
basics: Any consistent formal system with a checkable list of axioms that is strong enough to do arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. It also cannot prove its own consistency.
deeper: The proof encodes statements about proofs as numbers, then builds a sentence that says 'I am not provable here'. This limits dreams of a single complete rulebook for mathematics.
expert: Theorem I: consistent, recursively axiomatized T ⊇ PA ⇒ ∃ G_T true but T ⊬ G_T. Theorem II: T ⊬ Con(T).
regime: Applies to formal systems that can express arithmetic; says nothing against everyday reasoning or physical theories that are not axiomatic in this sense.

title: Calculus
basics: Calculus studies how quantities change (derivatives) and accumulate (integrals). It is the native language of motion, heat, waves and growth.
deeper: The fundamental theorem links the two operations: integrating a rate gives a net change. Limits make the infinitesimal idea rigorous.
expert: f′(x) = lim_{h→0}[f(x+h)−f(x)]/h;  ∫ₐᵇ f′ dx = f(b)−f(a);  Taylor: f(x)=Σ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)(x−a)ⁿ/n!
regime: Needs smooth-enough functions; discrete or fractal systems need other tools.
evidence: Two centuries of successful physical prediction

title: Differential equations (ODEs and PDEs)
basics: A differential equation relates a quantity to its own rates of change. Ordinary ones describe a few moving parts; partial ones describe fields and fluids that vary in space and time.
deeper: Most physical laws are of this form: given where a system is and how fast it is changing, the equation fixes the future. Few can be solved exactly, so numerical methods carry much of science.
expert: ODE: dy/dt = f(y,t). Heat: ∂u/∂t = α∇²u. Wave: ∂²u/∂t² = c²∇²u. Laplace: ∇²φ = 0.
regime: Existence and smoothness of solutions is not guaranteed for every nonlinear PDE (see Navier-Stokes).
evidence: Numerical weather, orbit and circuit prediction

title: Linear algebra and Hilbert spaces
basics: Vectors, matrices and linear maps give a way to handle many numbers at once. Quantum states live in a special vector space called a Hilbert space.
deeper: Eigenvalues and eigenvectors pick out the special directions a transformation only stretches. Observables in quantum theory are operators whose eigenvalues are the possible results.
expert: Aψ = λψ; ⟨φ|ψ⟩ inner product; unitary U†U = 1 preserves probability; SVD: A = UΣV†.
regime: Linear structure is exact in quantum mechanics but only approximate for most macroscopic systems.

title: Differential geometry
basics: Differential geometry describes curved spaces. It supplies the maths for general relativity, where gravity is the curvature of spacetime.
deeper: Locally a curved space looks flat; the metric tells you how to measure distances and angles, and curvature measures how parallel lines drift apart.
expert: ds² = g_μν dx^μ dx^ν; Christoffel Γ^λ_μν = ½g^{λσ}(∂_μ g_σν+∂_ν g_σμ−∂_σ g_μν); Riemann R^ρ_σμν.
regime: Smooth manifolds only; quantum-scale spacetime may not be a smooth manifold.

title: Group theory and symmetry
basics: A symmetry is a change that leaves something looking the same. Group theory classifies all such changes and explains why particles and crystals come in neat patterns.
deeper: Rotations, reflections and gauge transformations form groups. Particle families correspond to representations of groups such as SU(3), SU(2) and U(1).
expert: Standard Model gauge group SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y; 230 space groups classify crystals.
regime: Some symmetries are exact as far as we know (Poincaré invariance, colour SU(3)); others are broken (electroweak, flavour, crystal symmetries at a given temperature).
evidence: Eightfold way predicted the Ω⁻ baryon

title: Noether's theorem
basics: Every continuous symmetry of a physical law brings a conserved quantity. Same laws at all times gives energy conservation, same laws everywhere gives momentum conservation, same laws in all directions gives angular momentum conservation.
deeper: This explains why conservation laws exist rather than treating them as separate facts. The global phase symmetry of charged fields brings conservation of electric charge.
expert: If δL = ε dF/dt under q→q+εK, then Q = Σ(∂L/∂q̇)K − F is conserved on solutions of the equations of motion (dQ/dt = 0). Time shift → E; translation → p; rotation → L.
regime: Applies to systems with an action principle; energy is not globally conserved in an expanding universe.

title: Probability
basics: Probability measures how likely events are. It lets us reason about noise, chance, quantum outcomes and incomplete knowledge.
deeper: Random variables have distributions with means and variances. The law of large numbers and the central limit theorem explain why averages are so well behaved.
expert: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B); E[X]=Σxp(x); Var X=E[X²]−E[X]²; Normal: p(x)=e^{−(x−μ)²/2σ²}/(σ√2π).
regime: Needs a well-defined sample space; subjective vs frequentist readings differ.

title: Bayesian inference and statistics
basics: Statistics turns data into conclusions with stated uncertainty. Bayes' rule says how to update beliefs when new evidence arrives.
deeper: Sampling error shrinks as 1/√N, which is why more data narrows confidence intervals. Particle physics demands 5σ (about 1 in 3.5 million by chance) before announcing a discovery.
expert: P(H|D)=P(D|H)P(H)/P(D); CLT: x̄ ~ N(μ,σ²/N); 5σ ↔ p ≈ 2.9×10⁻⁷ (one-sided).
regime: Misuse (p-hacking, multiple comparisons) is a major source of unreliable claims.

title: Dynamical systems and chaos
basics: Simple rules can produce unpredictable behaviour. In chaotic systems, tiny differences in the starting state grow exponentially.
deeper: Orbits settle on attractors; bifurcations are sudden qualitative changes as a parameter moves. The Lorenz equations, a toy weather model, show a butterfly-shaped strange attractor.
expert: Lyapunov exponent λ>0: δ(t)≈δ₀e^{λt}. Logistic map xₙ₊₁=r xₙ(1−xₙ), chaos for r≳3.57. Lorenz: ẋ=σ(y−x), ẏ=x(ρ−z)−y, ż=xy−βz.
regime: Deterministic but practically unpredictable beyond a Lyapunov time.

title: Fourier analysis
basics: Almost any signal you meet in practice can be built by adding sine waves of different frequencies. This explains musical tones, image compression and why waves of different colours can be separated.
deeper: A function and its Fourier transform are two views of the same thing; narrow in one means broad in the other, which is the maths behind the uncertainty principle.
expert: f̂(k)=∫f(x)e^{−ikx}dx; Δx·Δk ≥ ½ (Δx, Δk the standard deviations of |f|² and |f̂|²).
regime: Linear systems; nonlinear systems mix frequencies.

title: Graphs and networks
basics: A graph is dots joined by lines. It is the standard way to describe the internet, food webs, neurons and social ties.
deeper: Key measures include degree, shortest paths and clustering. Many real networks are 'small-world' or have a few hugely connected hubs.
expert: Some networks have heavy-tailed degree distributions P(k)∼k^{−γ} (γ typically 2–3 when a power law fits), but strictly scale-free networks are rare (Broido & Clauset 2019). Erdős-Rényi: a giant component appears at ⟨k⟩=1.
regime: Real networks evolve, so static graph models are snapshots; whether degree distributions are truly power-law is contested.
evidence: Food web, protein-interaction and web-link studies

title: Open problems in mathematics
basics: Some of the deepest unanswered questions are in pure mathematics: the Riemann hypothesis, P versus NP, the Yang-Mills mass gap and whether fluid equations can blow up.
deeper: Several of these bear on cryptography, number theory and the foundations of computing and fluid modelling. The mass-gap problem asks for a rigorous proof of facts that experiments and computer lattice simulations already strongly suggest.
expert: Navier-Stokes: ∂ₜu+(u·∇)u=−∇p/ρ+ν∇²u, ∇·u=0 (smoothness for all time unproven in 3D unforced). RH: all nontrivial zeros of ζ(s) have Re s=½.
regime: Open as of the knowledge baseline; progress claims need peer review.

frontier.text: Yang-Mills mass gap has no rigorous proof though lattice QCD supports it

title: Newton's laws of motion
basics: An object keeps its velocity unless a force acts, acceleration equals the net force divided by mass, and for contact and gravitational forces they come in equal, opposite pairs. These rules explain everyday motion.
deeper: Newton's second law, together with a force law like gravity, lets you compute future paths. Forces are tied to interactions, not to objects 'wanting' to move.
expert: F = dp/dt = ma; F₁₂ = −F₂₁; p = mv.
regime: Fails for v ≈ c (relativity), tiny scales (quantum), and very strong gravity (GR).

title: Newtonian gravity
basics: Every mass attracts every other with a force that weakens with the square of the distance. It holds planets in orbit and makes things fall.
deeper: Near Earth the pull is about 9.8 m/s² for everything, regardless of mass. Newton's law was the first law to unite earthly and heavenly motion.
expert: F = G m₁m₂/r², G = 6.67430(15)×10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² (CODATA 2018); g = GM/R² ≈ 9.81 m/s²; v_esc = √(2GM/r).
regime: Breaks down near compact objects and at cosmological distances where general relativity matters.

title: Orbits and Kepler's laws
basics: Planets move on ellipses with the Sun at one focus, sweep equal areas in equal times, and take longer to orbit the farther out they are.
deeper: These laws follow from inverse-square gravity and angular momentum conservation. Orbital periods let astronomers weigh stars and planets.
expert: T² = 4π²a³/(G(M+m)); L = mr²θ̇ constant; vis-viva v² = GM(2/r−1/a).
regime: Small corrections from other bodies and relativity: Mercury's perihelion advances about 574″/century in total, and the 43″/century left after planetary perturbations is explained by GR.

title: Conservation of energy
basics: Energy changes form (motion, height, heat, light) but its total in an isolated system never changes. It is one of the most reliable rules in science.
deeper: Work done by forces moves energy between kinetic and potential forms; friction turns it into heat. Noether's theorem ties it to the laws being the same at all times.
expert: E = ½mv² + U; W = ∫F·dr; ΔKE = W_net; 1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻².
regime: Locally exact; in an expanding universe a global energy is not well defined.
evidence: Neutrino hypothesis rescued it in β decay

title: Momentum and collisions
basics: When objects collide or explode, their combined momentum (mass times velocity) is unchanged. Rockets and billiard balls both obey this.
deeper: Elastic collisions also conserve kinetic energy; inelastic ones lose some to heat or deformation. Impulse is force acting over time.
expert: Σp_before = Σp_after; J = ∫F dt = Δp; rocket: Δv = v_e ln(m₀/m₁).
regime: Exact in an isolated system at all scales (Noether), extended to p = γmv for relativity.
evidence: Collision experiments from labs to accelerators

title: Rotation and angular momentum
basics: Spinning things resist changes to their spin. Pull your arms in and you spin faster because angular momentum is conserved.
deeper: Torque changes angular momentum like force changes momentum. Gyroscopes, spinning planets and collapsing stars all use this.
expert: τ = dL/dt; L = Iω for rotation about a principal axis (in general L = 𝐈·ω, and L need not be parallel to ω); I = Σmr²; KE_rot = ½Iω².
regime: Relativistic and quantum versions add spin; classical formula fails for fundamental spin-½ particles.

title: Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics
basics: Instead of tracking forces, you can find the motion that makes a quantity called action stationary. This viewpoint generalises easily to fields and quantum theory.
deeper: Energy-based formulations make constraints and symmetries easy to handle. The Hamiltonian version is the direct ancestor of the Schrödinger equation.
expert: S=∫L dt, L=T−V; d/dt(∂L/∂q̇)=∂L/∂q; H=Σpq̇−L; q̇=∂H/∂p, ṗ=−∂H/∂q.
regime: Classical; the path-integral generalises it to quantum theory.
evidence: Equivalent to Newton for conservative systems

title: Oscillations and resonance
basics: Anything with a restoring force near equilibrium swings back and forth. Pushing at its natural frequency builds large oscillations (resonance).
deeper: Springs, pendulums, molecular bonds and electric circuits all share the same maths. Damping makes the swing die out.
expert: ẍ+ω₀²x=0, ω₀=√(k/m); damped driven: ẍ+2γẋ+ω₀²x=F cosΩt/m; Q=ω₀/2γ.
regime: Linear only for small amplitudes. The 1940 Tacoma Narrows collapse is often quoted as resonance, but it was self-excited aeroelastic flutter.
evidence: Driven pendulum and LC-circuit resonance curves

title: Waves and sound
basics: A wave carries energy and information without carrying matter along. Sound, water ripples and seismic shaking are all waves.
deeper: Waves interfere, reflect, refract and diffract. Speed depends on the medium: stiffer and lighter means faster.
expert: v=fλ; v_string=√(T/μ); v_sound,air≈331+0.6T(°C) m/s ≈ 343 m/s at 20 °C; I∝A²; Doppler f′=f(v±v_o)/(v∓v_s).
regime: Linear superposition holds for small amplitude; shocks form when it fails.

title: Stress, strain and elasticity
basics: For small stretches, solids stretch in proportion to the force; beyond the elastic limit they deform permanently or break. Stiffness comes from atomic bonds acting like tiny springs.
deeper: Young's modulus tells how stiff a material is. Beyond the elastic limit, defects move and the material yields.
expert: σ=Eε; E_steel≈200 GPa, E_rubber≈0.01–0.1 GPa; shear τ=Gγ; bulk B=−V dP/dV.
regime: Linear elasticity valid for small strains; plasticity and fracture need other models.

title: Atomic-scale springs (interatomic potentials)
basics: Atoms attract at moderate distances and repel when too close, so the energy has a minimum at the bond length. Near that minimum the bond acts like a spring.
deeper: The Lennard-Jones form, with an r⁻⁶ attraction (van der Waals) and a convenient r⁻¹² repulsion (really exclusion-principle overlap), is a common model for neutral atoms; covalent and ionic bonds use other curves such as the Morse potential. Such curves explain thermal expansion, stiffness and melting.
expert: V(r)=4ε[(σ/r)¹²−(σ/r)⁶]; minimum at r=2^{1/6}σ; k=V″(r₀).
regime: Classical approximation for neutral atoms; real bonds need quantum mechanics.

title: Pressure, buoyancy and Archimedes
basics: Pressure in a fluid grows with depth, and an object feels an upward push equal to the weight of fluid it displaces. That is why ships float and divers feel pressure.
deeper: Atmospheric pressure at sea level (≈101 kPa) is the weight of the air column above. Pascal's principle underlies hydraulic machines.
expert: P=P₀+ρgh; F_b=ρ_fluid V g; 1 atm = 101 325 Pa.
regime: Incompressible, static fluid assumed; ρ varies in gases.

title: Bernoulli's principle and lift
basics: In smoothly flowing fluid, faster flow goes with lower pressure. Wings turn the air downward; the pressure difference across the wing is how that momentum change pushes the wing up.
deeper: Newton's third law and Bernoulli's equation are two descriptions of the same momentum change. Stall happens when flow separates from the wing.
expert: P+½ρv²+ρgh=const along a streamline; L=½ρv²SC_L.
regime: Steady, incompressible, inviscid flow; fails with strong viscosity or shocks.

title: Navier-Stokes equations
basics: These equations say how a fluid's velocity changes because of pressure, viscosity and external forces. They govern air, water, blood and the weather.
deeper: Solutions are well tested, but whether they stay smooth forever in 3D is a famous unsolved problem. Practical simulations use numerical grids and turbulence models.
expert: Incompressible, constant-viscosity form: ρ(∂ₜu+u·∇u)=−∇p+μ∇²u+f; ∇·u=0; Re=ρUL/μ (compressible flows add a density equation and bulk viscosity).
regime: Continuum limit (length ≫ mean free path); non-Newtonian fluids need modified stress laws.
evidence: Pipe flow, aerodynamics and ocean models

title: Turbulence
basics: Fast flows break into swirling eddies of all sizes. Turbulence mixes heat and momentum very efficiently but has no complete first-principles theory.
deeper: Energy cascades from big eddies to small ones until viscosity turns it into heat. Kolmogorov's 1941 scaling predicts how the energy is spread over eddy sizes.
expert: E(k)=C ε^{2/3}k^{−5/3}, C≈1.5; Kolmogorov scale η=(ν³/ε)^{1/4}; Re_crit(pipe)≈2000–2300 (sustained turbulence near Re≈2040; laminar flow can persist far higher in very quiet conditions).
regime: The −5/3 spectrum is well supported in the 3D inertial range, but intermittency makes higher-order scaling exponents deviate from Kolmogorov's 1941 values; exact closure is unsolved.

frontier.text: No first-principles derivation of turbulence statistics

title: Temperature and heat
basics: Temperature tells which way heat flows; for a dilute gas it is proportional to the average random kinetic energy of the molecules. Heat is energy moving because of a temperature difference.
deeper: Heat flows by conduction, convection and radiation. Materials differ in how much heat they need to warm up (specific heat).
expert: Q=mcΔT; q=−k∇T; P_rad=εσAT⁴, σ=5.670×10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴; Wien λ_max T=2.898×10⁻³ m K.
regime: Local equilibrium assumed; temperature is undefined far from equilibrium.

title: Heat conduction and diffusion
basics: Heat and dissolved particles spread out from hot or concentrated regions to cooler or emptier ones, driven by random motion.
deeper: The same equation describes cooling coffee, ink in water and the slow flow of heat through Earth's crust. The spread grows as the square root of time.
expert: ∂u/∂t=D∇²u; ⟨x²⟩=2Dt in one dimension (⟨r²⟩=2nDt in n dimensions); Fick J=−D∇c.
regime: Valid when transport is diffusive, not ballistic.

title: Kinetic theory of gases
basics: Gas pressure comes from countless molecules bouncing off walls. Temperature is a measure of how energetic those motions are.
deeper: The ideal-gas law follows from this picture. Real gases deviate when molecules attract or take up space.
expert: PV=NkT=nRT; ⟨½mv²⟩=3/2 kT; v_rms=√(3kT/m); R=8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; k=1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K.
regime: Dilute, high-temperature limit; van der Waals corrections otherwise.

title: First law of thermodynamics
basics: Energy is conserved when heat and work are both counted: heat added to a system either warms it or lets it do work.
deeper: It forbids machines that output more energy than they take in. Internal energy is stored in the random motion and interactions of particles.
expert: ΔU=Q−W; dU=TdS−PdV; C_p−C_v=R (ideal gas).
regime: Universal for macroscopic systems.

title: Second law and entropy
basics: In an isolated system entropy (a count of the microscopic arrangements that look the same as what we see) tends to increase. This gives time its arrow and explains why heat flows from hot to cold.
deeper: Entropy counts how many microscopic arrangements match what we see. Local order (like life) is possible only by exporting entropy.
expert: dS≥δQ/T; S=k_B ln W (k_B=1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K); η_Carnot=1−T_c/T_h.
regime: Statistical law, essentially exact for macroscopic systems; fluctuation theorems cover tiny systems.

frontier.text: Why the early universe had very low entropy is unexplained

title: Third law and absolute zero
basics: You cannot reach absolute zero in a finite number of steps. Entropy of a perfect crystal approaches zero at 0 K.
deeper: Cooling gets harder near zero because heat capacities and entropy differences between states vanish, so every cooling step gains less than the last. Quantum effects like superfluidity appear at very low temperature.
expert: S→0 as T→0 (perfect crystal); 0 K=−273.15 °C.
regime: Residual entropy exists for disordered solids like ice.

title: Statistical mechanics
basics: Statistical mechanics derives the laws of heat from the random motion of huge numbers of atoms. It is the main bridge from microscopic to macroscopic.
deeper: At equilibrium each microstate with energy E has probability proportional to e^(−E/kT); a set of states sharing an energy is weighted by how many there are. Averaging over this distribution gives pressure, heat capacity and magnetisation.
expert: p_i=e^{−E_i/kT}/Z; Z=Σe^{−E_i/kT}; F=−kT ln Z; S=−k Σp ln p.
regime: Needs many particles and ergodic mixing; small or driven systems need fluctuation theorems.

title: Heat engines and refrigerators
basics: Engines turn heat into work by moving heat from hot to cold, and the second law caps their efficiency. Refrigerators run the same process in reverse using work.
deeper: Real car engines (Otto cycle) and power plants (Rankine cycle) reach well below the Carnot limit because of friction and finite-speed heat flow.
expert: η≤1−T_c/T_h; Otto η=1−r^{1−γ}; COP_fridge=T_c/(T_h−T_c).
regime: Cycle models idealise combustion; irreversibility cuts real efficiency.

title: Phase transitions and critical phenomena
basics: Matter changes phase (melting, boiling, magnetising) abruptly when conditions cross a threshold. Near critical points many different systems behave in the same universal way.
deeper: Phase transitions are collective effects: no single molecule 'melts'. Universality means details drop out near a critical point.
expert: Clausius-Clapeyron dP/dT=L/(TΔv); order parameter ∼|T−T_c|^β; 3D Ising β≈0.326.
regime: Mean-field theory fails near T_c in low dimension.

title: Thermal radiation and blackbody spectrum
basics: Hot objects glow, and the colour depends only on temperature. This is why a heated metal goes red then white and why stars have colours.
deeper: Planck explained the spectrum in 1900 by assuming the oscillators in the cavity walls exchange energy only in units hf; Einstein (1905) extended the idea to light itself. This started quantum theory. The Sun's surface (5772 K) peaks in the visible.
expert: B_λ=(2hc²/λ⁵)/(e^{hc/λkT}−1); h=6.62607×10⁻³⁴ J s; L=4πR²σT⁴.
regime: Ideal for opaque bodies; real objects have emissivity<1.

title: Electric charge and Coulomb's law
basics: Like charges repel and opposite charges attract, with a force that weakens with distance squared. This force holds atoms and molecules together.
deeper: The electric force between a proton and electron is about 10³⁹ times stronger than their gravity. Free charge is quantised in units of e (quarks carry e/3 and 2e/3 but are never found free).
regime: Static point charges; moving charges need full electrodynamics.

title: Electric fields, potential and capacitance
basics: A charge sets up an electric field that pushes other charges. Voltage is the energy per unit charge, and capacitors store charge by holding a field between plates.
deeper: Gauss's law relates field flux to enclosed charge. Conductors in equilibrium have no internal field, shielding what is inside.
expert: E=F/q; ∮E·dA=Q/ε₀; V=−∫E·dl; C=Q/V=ε₀A/d; U=½CV².
regime: Classical fields; quantised at the photon level.

title: Circuits, Ohm's law and Kirchhoff's rules
basics: Current is charge flow, and in many materials it is proportional to the voltage across them. Circuit rules let you predict how currents split and voltages drop.
deeper: Resistance comes from electrons scattering off lattice vibrations and defects. Power dissipated as heat is voltage times current.
expert: V=IR; P=IV=I²R; Kirchhoff ΣI=0 at nodes, ΣV=0 around loops; RC time constant τ=RC.
regime: Ohmic materials; the loop rule needs no changing magnetic flux; diodes and transistors are nonlinear.

title: Magnetic fields and forces
basics: Moving charges feel a sideways force in a magnetic field, and moving charges also make magnetic fields. Compass needles, motors and particle accelerators rely on this.
deeper: Magnetism is a relativistic companion of electricity: what is magnetic in one frame partly looks electric in another. Permanent magnets come from aligned electron spins.
expert: F=q(E+v×B); r=mv/(qB); ∮B·dl=μ₀I; μ₀≈1.2566×10⁻⁶ N/A².
regime: Classical; single-spin magnetism is quantum.

title: Electromagnetic induction
basics: A changing magnetic field creates an electric field. This is how generators produce electricity and transformers change voltage.
deeper: Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change that caused it, which is energy conservation in action.
expert: ε=−dΦ_B/dt; transformer V_s/V_p=N_s/N_p; L: ε=−L dI/dt; X_L=ωL.
regime: Classical; exact within Maxwell theory.

title: Maxwell's equations
basics: Four equations describe all classical electric and magnetic phenomena, and show that light is an electromagnetic wave.
deeper: They unified electricity, magnetism and optics in 1865 and led to special relativity. The speed of the waves comes out from constants measured in the lab.
regime: Classical; QED supersedes it for single photons and strong fields.

title: Electromagnetic waves and spectrum
basics: Light, radio, microwaves, X-rays and gamma rays are the same kind of wave differing only in wavelength. They carry energy through empty space at the speed of light.
deeper: The visible band is a sliver between 380 and 750 nm. Photon energy rises as wavelength falls, so gamma rays ionise atoms while radio waves do not.
expert: c=fλ; E_photon=hf=hc/λ ≈ 1240 eV nm/λ; Poynting S=E×B/μ₀.
regime: Wave picture for many photons; particle picture for single events.

title: Geometric optics and lenses
basics: Light rays bend when entering glass or water, which lets lenses form images in cameras, eyes and telescopes.
deeper: Refraction follows Snell's law; total internal reflection traps light in optical fibre. Aberrations limit simple lenses.
expert: n₁sinθ₁=n₂sinθ₂; 1/f=1/d_o+1/d_i; lensmaker 1/f=(n−1)(1/R₁−1/R₂); n_water=1.33, n_glass≈1.5.
regime: Valid when features ≫ wavelength.

title: Interference, diffraction and polarisation
basics: Light waves add and cancel to make bright and dark fringes, and spread around obstacles. This shows light's wave nature and sets the limit on how fine an image can be.
deeper: Slit patterns reveal wavelength; thin films and soap bubbles show colour from interference. Polarisation selects the wave's oscillation direction.
expert: d sinθ=mλ (double-slit bright fringes, m=0,±1,…); a sinθ=mλ (single-slit dark minima, m=±1,±2,…); Rayleigh limit θ=1.22λ/D; Malus I=I₀cos²θ.
regime: Scalar/Maxwell wave theory; needs quantum treatment for single-photon statistics.

title: Projectiles and free fall
basics: Thrown objects follow curved paths because gravity pulls them down while their sideways motion continues. Without air, all objects fall equally fast.
deeper: Horizontal and vertical motion are independent. Air drag adds a terminal speed, which is why raindrops do not hit like bullets.
expert: y=v₀t sinθ−½gt²; range=v₀² sin2θ/g (launch and landing at the same height, uniform g, no drag); terminal v_t=√(2mg/ρC_dA).
regime: Uniform g and no spin or drag assumed.

title: Rockets and spaceflight
basics: Rockets move by throwing mass backwards, and the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation says how much fuel it takes to change speed.
deeper: Most of a rocket is propellant. Orbiting needs about 7.8 km/s sideways at low Earth altitude, not just height.
expert: Δv=v_e ln(m₀/m_f); v_circ=√(GM/r)≈7.7–7.8 km/s (LEO, 200–400 km); v_esc(Earth)=11.2 km/s.
regime: Chemical rockets limited by exhaust speed ≈ 3–4.5 km/s.

title: Special relativity
basics: The speed of light is the same for every observer, so time and space measurements depend on motion. Moving clocks run slow and length contracts.
deeper: Mass and energy are interchangeable, and nothing with mass can reach light speed. The theory combines space and time into one four-dimensional spacetime.
expert: γ=1/√(1−v²/c²); Δt=γΔt₀; E²=(pc)²+(mc²)²; E=mc² at rest; 1 u=931.494 MeV/c².
regime: Exact in flat spacetime (no gravity) and valid locally in GR; tested at all speeds up to those of cosmic rays and LHC protons.

title: General relativity
basics: Gravity is the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy, and objects follow the straightest paths through that curved geometry. It extends Newton's gravity to strong fields and cosmic distances.
deeper: Its predictions include light bending, gravitational time dilation, gravitational waves and black holes. All precision tests so far agree with it.
expert: G_μν+Λg_μν=(8πG/c⁴)T_μν; Schwarzschild r_s=2GM/c²; Mercury precession 42.98″/century.
regime: Tested from the laboratory to solar-system and astrophysical scales (cosmological tests are weaker); expected to fail at singularities and the Planck scale.

frontier.text: Singularities signal where GR breaks down

title: Relativity in GPS
basics: GPS satellite clocks run at different rates than ground clocks, and the system would drift by kilometres a day if it ignored relativity.
deeper: Speed slows the clocks by about 7 microseconds per day while weaker gravity speeds them up by about 45, a net gain of about 38.
expert: Δt_total≈+45.7−7.2≈+38.5 μs/day; orbital radius ≈26 560 km.
regime: Small corrections; classical models fail only through accumulated drift.

title: Gravitational lensing
basics: Mass bends the path of light passing near it, so galaxies and clusters can magnify and distort the images of objects behind them.
deeper: Lensing measures mass whether or not it shines, which is a key piece of the dark matter evidence.
expert: α=4GM/(c²b); Einstein radius θ_E=√(4GM D_ds/(c²D_dD_s)).
regime: Weak-field limit of GR.

title: Gravitational waves
basics: Accelerating masses ripple spacetime. Detectors like LIGO sense stretches smaller than a proton in arms several kilometres long.
deeper: The first detected merger (2015) matched GR waveforms for two ~30 solar-mass black holes. Mergers of neutron stars also emit light, enabling multi-messenger astronomy.
expert: h≈ΔL/L∼10⁻²¹; v=c; chirp mass ℳ=(m₁m₂)^{3/5}/(m₁+m₂)^{1/5}; peak luminosity of GW150914 ≈3.6×10⁴⁹ W ≈10⁻³ c⁵/G (c⁵/G≈3.6×10⁵² W is the natural scale, not the typical value).
regime: Linear weak-field regime for the propagation; strong-field merger needs numerical relativity.

title: Black holes
basics: A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can leave. They form when massive stars collapse and also sit at the centres of galaxies.
deeper: The edge, the event horizon, is not a surface but a one-way boundary. Black holes are described by mass, spin and charge, and spin is thought to power jets (the Blandford-Znajek mechanism is the leading model).
expert: r_s=2GM/c²≈2.95 km (M/M☉); T_H=ħc³/(8πGMk_B)≈6×10⁻⁸ K (M☉/M); S=k_Bc³A/(4Għ).
regime: Hawking radiation is predicted but unobserved; interior and information fate depend on quantum gravity.
evidence: EHT M87 and Sgr A* images

title: Origins of quantum theory
basics: Around 1900 blackbody light, the photoelectric effect and atomic spectra could not be explained by classical physics. Planck and Einstein proposed that energy comes in discrete packets.
deeper: Bohr's atom, de Broglie's matter waves and then Heisenberg and Schrödinger's mechanics replaced the old picture by 1926.
expert: E=hf; photoelectric K_max=hf−φ; de Broglie λ=h/p.
regime: Historical; modern theory supersedes the 'old quantum theory'.

title: Wave-particle duality
basics: Light and matter show both wave and particle behaviour: electrons make interference patterns but are always detected one at a time.
deeper: Each particle is described by a wave of probability. The pattern builds up from single events even when particles pass through the apparatus one at a time.
expert: λ=h/p; electron at 100 eV: λ≈0.12 nm; two-slit fringe spacing Δy=λL/d.
regime: Universal; wave behaviour only observable when λ is comparable to apparatus features.

title: Schrödinger equation and the wave function
basics: The Schrödinger equation says how a quantum system's wave function changes in time. The square of the wave function gives the probability of finding the particle.
deeper: Solving it for an electron near a nucleus gives the allowed energy levels of atoms. Bound states are quantised because waves must fit in the space available.
expert: iħ∂ψ/∂t=Ĥψ; Ĥ=−ħ²∇²/2m+V; P=|ψ|²; ħ=1.0546×10⁻³⁴ J s; particle in a box E_n=n²π²ħ²/2mL².
regime: Non-relativistic, single-particle form; QFT handles creation of particles.
evidence: Hydrogen energy levels (Rydberg series, to about 10⁻⁵ relative accuracy; finer detail needs the Dirac equation and QED)

title: Uncertainty principle
basics: You cannot know both a particle's position and momentum exactly at the same time. This is a property of nature, not a limit of instruments.
deeper: It is why electrons do not fall into the nucleus and why a confined particle has minimum motion (zero-point energy).
expert: ΔxΔp≥ħ/2 (Kennard, standard deviations); energy-time: ΔE·τ≳ħ/2, where τ is the time over which the state changes appreciably; zero-point energy E₀=½ħω.
regime: Universal; follows from wave nature (Fourier).
evidence: Single-slit diffraction of electrons and neutrons (width-momentum spread)

title: Spin and the Pauli exclusion principle
basics: Particles carry an intrinsic angular momentum called spin. Two identical electrons cannot share the same quantum state, which forces atoms into shells.
deeper: Exclusion makes matter occupy space and holds up white dwarfs and neutron stars. Spin-statistics theorem sorts particles into fermions and bosons.
expert: s=½ (electron), g≈2.00232; fermions antisymmetric ψ(1,2)=−ψ(2,1); Fermi energy E_F=(ħ²/2m)(3π²n)^{2/3}.
regime: Exact for identical particles; the spin-statistics theorem is proven in relativistic QFT in 3+1 dimensions, while quasi-particles in 2D can be anyons.

title: Entanglement and Bell tests
basics: Two particles can share one quantum state so that measuring one instantly fixes correlations with the other, however far apart. No signal travels faster than light.
deeper: Bell's theorem showed that no local hidden-variable theory can match quantum correlations. Experiments, including loophole-free ones in 2015, agree with quantum mechanics.
expert: CHSH: |S|≤2 classically, quantum max 2√2≈2.83; singlet correlation E(a,b)=−cos(a−b).
regime: Exact within quantum theory; interpretation open.

frontier.text: Which interpretation of quantum mechanics is correct (non-local hidden variables, many-worlds, collapse models) is open; Bell tests rule out local hidden variables only.

title: Quantum tunnelling
basics: A particle can pass through an energy barrier that classically it could not climb. Tunnelling makes the Sun shine, flash memory work and radioactive alpha decay happen.
deeper: The chance falls exponentially with barrier width and particle mass, so electrons tunnel readily but cats do not.
expert: T≈e^{−2κa}, κ=√(2m(V₀−E))/ħ; Gamow factor for fusion e^{−2πη}.
regime: Wave-mechanical effect; WKB formula is an approximation.

title: Measurement problem and interpretations
basics: Quantum theory predicts probabilities extremely well, but why a single definite result appears when we measure is still debated. Several interpretations give identical predictions.
deeper: Main options: Copenhagen (collapse on measurement), many-worlds (no collapse, branching), Bohmian pilot waves, objective collapse models, and relational or Bayesian readings.
expert: Born rule p_i=|⟨i|ψ⟩|²; decoherence ρ→Σ_i p_i|i⟩⟨i| suppresses off-diagonal terms on timescale τ_D.
regime: The formalism is C1; which interpretation is right is untested. Collapse models make slightly different predictions that are being constrained.

frontier.text: Can any experiment distinguish interpretations (for example collapse-model heating or X-ray emission bounds)?
Objective collapse models are being tested

title: Decoherence and the quantum-classical boundary
basics: Interaction with surroundings quickly scrambles the delicate phase relations that make quantum effects visible. That is why everyday objects look classical.
deeper: Larger and warmer systems decohere faster. This is also the main obstacle for quantum computers.
expert: τ_D≈τ_R(λ_T/Δx)², λ_T=ħ/√(2mk_BT) (Zurek's estimate; order of magnitude only); coherence times: superconducting qubits ~10⁻⁴ s, trapped ions >1 s.
regime: Explains apparent collapse but does not by itself solve the measurement problem.

frontier.text: What is the largest object that can be kept in a quantum superposition, and does any collapse mechanism set a limit?

title: Quantum electrodynamics
basics: QED describes light and charged matter as quantum fields exchanging photons. It is the most precisely tested theory in science.
deeper: The electron's magnetic moment is measured to about 1 part in 10¹² and agrees with QED, given the fine-structure constant measured independently. Virtual particles are bookkeeping for terms in the calculation.
regime: Perturbative in α; incomplete without weak and strong forces.

title: The Standard Model of particle physics
basics: The Standard Model lists the known elementary particles (quarks, leptons, force carriers and the Higgs) and three of the four forces. It is tested to extraordinary precision but is known to be incomplete.
deeper: It has 12 matter particles in three generations and gauge bosons for the strong, weak and electromagnetic forces. It omits gravity, dark matter and neutrino masses as normally written.
expert: Gauge group SU(3)_C×SU(2)_L×U(1)_Y; ~19 free parameters (more with neutrino masses); m_W=80.377 GeV (PDG average; CDF 2022 measured 80.434 GeV, in tension), m_Z=91.19 GeV, m_H≈125 GeV.
regime: Valid up to at least TeV energies; new physics must exist for gravity and dark matter.

frontier.text: What explains dark matter and neutrino masses, and why is the W-mass measurement from CDF in tension with the other results?

title: Quarks and leptons
basics: Ordinary matter is built from up and down quarks and electrons. Heavier copies of these exist in two more generations and are produced in cosmic rays and accelerators.
deeper: Quarks come in six flavours with fractional charge; leptons include the electron, muon, tau and three neutrinos. Quarks are never seen alone.
regime: Point-like down to <10⁻¹⁸ m; why three generations is unknown.

title: Quantum chromodynamics and confinement
basics: QCD is the theory of the strong force, in which quarks carry 'colour' and exchange gluons. The force does not weaken with distance, so quarks are locked inside protons and neutrons.
deeper: Most of a proton's mass comes from the energy of this strongly interacting field, not the quark masses. At very short distances quarks behave almost freely (asymptotic freedom).
expert: L=−¼G^a_μνG^{aμν}+Σq̄(iD̸−m)q; α_s(M_Z)=0.118; string tension ≈1 GeV/fm; m_p=938.27 MeV/c².
regime: Perturbative at high energy; non-perturbative regime solved numerically (lattice QCD).

frontier.text: Rigorous proof of the mass gap is missing

title: Higgs field and electroweak symmetry breaking
basics: A field filling space gives mass to W and Z bosons and to the fundamental matter particles. The Higgs boson, found in 2012, is a ripple of that field.
deeper: It explains why the weak force is short-range, but not why particle masses have their pattern. Only a small part of everyday mass comes from the Higgs.
regime: Measured couplings (W, Z, top, bottom, tau, muon) agree with the Standard Model at the ~5–25 % level; the charm, light-quark and self-couplings are not yet measured precisely.

frontier.text: Why the Higgs mass is so light (hierarchy problem)

title: Neutrinos and their masses
basics: Neutrinos are nearly massless particles that barely interact. About 60 billion solar neutrinos pass through every square centimetre each second, so several hundred trillion pass through a person every second, and they change type (flavour) as they travel.
deeper: Flavour oscillation proves they have mass, which the original Standard Model lacked. Their absolute mass scale and whether they are their own antiparticles remain unknown.
expert: Two-flavour approximation: P(ν_α→ν_β)=sin²2θ·sin²(1.27 Δm²[eV²]·L[km]/E[GeV]); the real three-flavour case adds matter effects and a CP phase. Δm²₂₁≈7.5×10⁻⁵ eV², |Δm²₃₁|≈2.5×10⁻³ eV²; Σm_ν<0.07–0.12 eV (95 %, ΛCDM, model-dependent); direct limit m_νe<0.45 eV (KATRIN 2024).
regime: Oscillation parameters well measured; ordering and absolute scale open.

title: Antimatter and the matter-antimatter imbalance
basics: Every particle has an antiparticle (some, like the photon, are their own), yet the universe contains almost only matter. The Standard Model's tiny CP violation cannot explain the imbalance.
deeper: Sakharov listed three conditions for creating a net excess: baryon-number violation, C and CP violation, and departure from equilibrium. Leptogenesis and electroweak baryogenesis are leading ideas.
expert: η=(n_B−n_B̄)/n_γ≈6×10⁻¹⁰; Jarlskog invariant J≈3×10⁻⁵.
regime: SM CP violation gives η too small by orders of magnitude.

title: Strong CP problem and axions
basics: QCD allows a CP-violating term, yet the neutron's electric dipole moment is tiny. The axion is a proposed particle that would explain it and could also be dark matter.
deeper: The strong CP problem is real (the neutron dipole moment is tiny), but the axion solution is hypothetical and undetected. Axion searches use strong magnetic fields to convert them into microwave photons.
expert: |θ̄|<10⁻¹⁰ (from d_n<1.8×10⁻²⁶ e cm); axion mass m_a≈5.7 μeV (10¹²GeV/f_a).
regime: Hypothetical; no detection yet.

title: Spontaneous symmetry breaking
basics: A system can have symmetric laws yet settle into a lopsided state, like a pencil balanced on its tip falling in some direction. This explains magnets, superconductors and how some particles get mass.
deeper: Goldstone modes appear when a continuous symmetry breaks; in gauge theories they are absorbed to give mass (Higgs mechanism).
regime: Applies from condensed matter to particle physics.

title: Quantum gravity
basics: General relativity and quantum theory clash where gravity becomes strong at tiny scales, around the Planck length. No tested theory yet unites them.
deeper: Main programmes are string theory, loop quantum gravity, asymptotic safety and causal sets. Tests would need tiny effects such as gravitational-wave echoes or lab entanglement via gravity.
regime: Speculative; no experiment yet probes ℓ_P.

title: Black hole information paradox
basics: Hawking's calculation suggested black holes destroy information, clashing with quantum theory. Recent calculations suggest information escapes in subtle correlations.
deeper: The 'Page curve' and 'island' calculations point to unitary evolution, but a full mechanism is not settled.
expert: S_BH=A/4ℓ_P²; evaporation time t≈5120πG²M³/(ħc⁴).
regime: Theoretical; requires quantum gravity.

title: Protons and neutrons
basics: Protons and neutrons are each made of three valence quarks plus a sea of gluons and quark-antiquark pairs, with a charge radius of about 0.84 femtometres. The neutron is slightly heavier and decays outside nuclei.
deeper: Most of their mass is energy of the strong field. Measurements of the proton radius from muonic hydrogen and electron scattering have largely converged.
expert: m_p=938.272 MeV/c², m_n=939.565 MeV/c²; r_p≈0.84 fm (charge radius); τ_n≈878.4 s (PDG); bottle ≈877.8 s, beam ≈888 s, a gap of ~10 s.
regime: Composite particles; probe energies above ~1 GeV resolve quarks.

title: Nuclear force and nuclear structure
basics: A short-range attraction between nucleons holds protons and neutrons together against electric repulsion. Nuclei are roughly 10,000 to 100,000 times smaller than atoms.
deeper: Stable nuclei have a balance of neutrons and protons, with magic numbers (2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126) of extra stability.
expert: R=r₀A^{1/3}, r₀≈1.2 fm; nuclear density ≈2.3×10¹⁷ kg/m³; range ~1–2 fm.
regime: Effective description of residual QCD forces.

title: Nuclear binding energy
basics: The mass of a nucleus is less than the sum of its parts; the missing mass is the energy that binds it. Binding per nucleon peaks near iron, so both fusion of light nuclei and fission of heavy ones release energy.
deeper: The semi-empirical mass formula captures the balance of volume, surface, electric repulsion and pairing effects.
expert: B/A peaks ≈8.8 MeV at ⁵⁶Fe/⁶²Ni; B=a_vA−a_sA^{2/3}−a_cZ²/A^{1/3}−a_a(A−2Z)²/A±δ; fission of U-235 ≈200 MeV.
regime: Liquid-drop model is approximate; shell effects matter near magic numbers.
evidence: Atomic mass evaluation tables (AME2020) of measured nuclear masses

title: Radioactive decay and half-life
basics: Unstable nuclei decay at random but with a fixed average rate, shown by a half-life. Alpha, beta and gamma are the main types.
deeper: Alpha decay is tunnelling; beta decay changes a neutron into a proton via the weak force. Half-lives range from less than a microsecond to far longer than the age of the universe (for example Te-128, ~10²⁴ years).
expert: N=N₀e^{−λt}, t_{1/2}=ln2/λ; ¹⁴C 5730 y; ²³⁸U 4.468 Gy; ⁴⁰K 1.25 Gy.
regime: Statistical; individual decay times unpredictable.

title: Weak interaction
basics: The weak force changes one type of quark or lepton into another. It drives beta decay and the first step of fusion in the Sun.
deeper: It is carried by massive W and Z bosons, which makes it short-ranged and weak at low energy. It violates mirror symmetry (parity).
expert: G_F=1.166×10⁻⁵ GeV⁻²; n→p+e⁻+ν̄ₑ; Wu experiment 1957 (parity violation).
regime: Unified with electromagnetism above ~100 GeV.

title: Radiometric dating
basics: Counting how much of a radioactive isotope has decayed into its product dates rocks and fossils. Different isotope pairs cover timescales from thousands to billions of years.
deeper: Uranium-lead dates zircon crystals; carbon-14 dates organic remains back to ~50,000 years once calibrated against tree-ring and other records (IntCal20). Meteorites give Earth's age.
expert: t=(1/λ)ln(1+D/P); age of Earth 4.54±0.05 Gyr (Pb-Pb); oldest zircons ≈4.4 Gyr.
regime: Needs a system that stayed closed. Isochron and concordia methods can solve for the starting ratio, while simple parent-daughter methods must assume it.

title: Nuclear fission and reactors
basics: A heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 splits after absorbing a neutron, releasing about 200 MeV and more neutrons that sustain a chain reaction.
deeper: Reactors control the chain with absorbers and moderators and use the heat to make steam. Waste remains radioactive for long times.
expert: n+²³⁵U→fragments+2.4 n+~200 MeV; k_eff=1 critical; 1 kg ²³⁵U fission ≈8×10¹³ J.
regime: Engineering is mature; economics and waste policy are debated.

title: Nuclear fusion
basics: Light nuclei combine and release energy when pushed together at extreme temperatures. Fusion powers the Sun and other stars on the main sequence and giant branches.
deeper: Protons must tunnel through electric repulsion; this makes fusion slow and steady in the Sun. In reactors deuterium and tritium fuse more easily.
expert: pp chain: 4¹H→⁴He+2e⁺+2ν+26.7 MeV; D+T→⁴He(3.5 MeV)+n(14.1 MeV); ~0.7 % of mass converted.
regime: Power-plant fusion not yet achieved; NIF reached ignition in December 2022 (3.15 MJ fusion yield from 2.05 MJ of laser energy on target), though the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid.

title: Atomic structure and orbitals
basics: Electrons in atoms occupy fuzzy regions called orbitals, each with a fixed energy. Atoms emit or absorb light only when electrons jump between levels.
deeper: Orbitals are described by quantum numbers n, l, m and spin. Orbital shape (s, p, d, f) determines bond directions in molecules.
expert: E_n=−13.606 eV/n²; Bohr radius a₀=0.0529 nm; ΔE=hf; shells hold 2n² electrons.
regime: Exactly solvable for hydrogen in the Schrödinger model; fine structure, the Lamb shift and hyperfine splitting need relativity and QED. Multi-electron atoms require approximations (Hartree-Fock, DFT).

title: Atomic spectra and lasers
basics: Each element emits and absorbs light at its own set of wavelengths, a fingerprint. Lasers make coherent light by stimulating many atoms to emit together.
deeper: Spectra reveal what stars are made of. Stimulated emission with population inversion produces laser light, used from surgery to fibre communications.
expert: 1/λ=R_H(1/n₁²−1/n₂²), R_H=1.097×10⁷ m⁻¹; Einstein A, B coefficients; laser gain requires N₂>N₁.
regime: Fine and hyperfine structure add small splittings.

title: Scattering, absorption and sky colour
basics: Air molecules scatter short wavelengths far more than long ones, so the sky is blue and sunsets are red. Clouds look white because droplets scatter all colours equally.
deeper: Rayleigh scattering applies when particles are far smaller than the wavelength; larger drops give Mie scattering.
expert: Rayleigh I∝λ⁻⁴; blue (450 nm) scatters ≈6× more than red (700 nm), since (700/450)⁴ ≈ 5.9.
regime: Single-scattering limit; multiple scattering in thick clouds.

title: The periodic table
basics: Elements arranged by atomic number repeat their chemical behaviour in a periodic pattern, because electron shells fill in a regular order.
deeper: Main-group elements in the same column have the same number of outer electrons; transition metals follow looser patterns. Trends in size, ionisation energy and electronegativity follow from effective nuclear charge.
expert: Aufbau order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p…; Z_eff=Z−S; first ionisation energy H 13.6 eV, He 24.6 eV, Na 5.14 eV.
regime: Aufbau has exceptions (Cr, Cu); heavy elements show relativistic effects (gold colour).

title: Atomic clocks and tests of constants
basics: Optical atomic clocks count light cycles from atoms and are accurate to about one second in the age of the universe. They test whether constants drift and may detect dark matter.
deeper: The SI second is defined by caesium-133 hyperfine transition at 9 192 631 770 Hz.
expert: Fractional uncertainty ~10⁻¹⁸; Δν/ν sensitivity to α-variation; Sr lattice at 429 THz.
regime: No variation of constants found within current limits. GPS satellites carry microwave clocks; optical clocks test gravitational redshift but do not underlie GPS.
evidence: Comparisons of Sr, Yb and Al⁺ clocks

frontier.text: Which optical transition will replace caesium in the SI second, and when (a decision expected around 2030)?

title: Antihydrogen
basics: Antimatter atoms made at CERN have the same spectrum as hydrogen so far. A 2023 test (ALPHA-g) found they fall downward, consistent with ordinary gravity to about 25 % precision.
deeper: Studying antihydrogen tests CPT symmetry and the equivalence principle for antimatter.
expert: 1S-2S transition measured to ~2×10⁻¹² relative precision, consistent with hydrogen.
regime: Few atoms available per experiment.

frontier.text: Does antihydrogen fall with exactly the same acceleration as hydrogen (measured only to tens of percent so far)?

title: Chemical bonding
basics: Atoms bond by sharing or transferring electrons to lower their total energy. The main types are ionic, covalent and metallic, with weaker hydrogen bonds and van der Waals forces between molecules.
deeper: Electronegativity difference tells whether electrons are shared evenly (nonpolar), unevenly (polar) or transferred (ionic). All chemistry is electromagnetism acting through quantum mechanics.
expert: C–C 348 kJ/mol, C=C 614, C≡C 839, O–H 463; NaCl lattice energy ≈787 kJ/mol; Pauling χ(F)=3.98, χ(Na)=0.93.
regime: Bond models are classifications along a continuum.

title: Molecular geometry and orbitals (VSEPR, MO theory)
basics: Electron pairs repel each other, so molecules adopt shapes such as bent water or tetrahedral methane. Molecular orbital theory spreads electrons over whole molecules.
deeper: Hybridisation (sp, sp², sp³) is a way to describe bond directions. Delocalised orbitals explain benzene's stability and the colour of dyes.
expert: Bond angles: CH₄ 109.5°, H₂O 104.5°, NH₃ 107°; bond order=(n_bonding−n_antibonding)/2.
regime: VSEPR is qualitative; heavy-element and transition-metal compounds often deviate.

title: Intermolecular forces and hydrogen bonding
basics: Neutral molecules still attract each other through temporary and permanent charge imbalances. Hydrogen bonds are especially strong and shape water, proteins and DNA.
deeper: These forces set boiling points, solubility and how proteins fold. London dispersion forces arise from fluctuating electron clouds.
expert: H-bond ≈ 5–30 kJ/mol (water ≈ 21); dispersion ∝ r⁻⁶; boiling points: CH₄ 112 K, H₂O 373 K.
regime: Pairwise-additive models are approximate.

title: Why water is special (and why ice floats)
basics: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds, which give it a high boiling point, large heat capacity and strong solvent power. Ice is less dense than liquid water because bonds lock molecules into an open lattice.
deeper: Floating ice insulates lakes so life can survive winter. Water's density maximum near 4 °C makes lakes freeze from the top; its high heat capacity and latent heats moderate climate.
expert: ρ_ice=917 kg/m³, ρ_water(4 °C)=1000; c_p=4.18 J g⁻¹K⁻¹ (25 °C); L_fus=334 J/g (0 °C), L_vap=2257 J/g (100 °C); dielectric constant ≈80 (20 °C), 78 (25 °C).
regime: Anomalies fade at high temperature and in confinement.

title: States of matter and gases
basics: Matter exists as solid, liquid, gas and plasma depending on how strongly particles interact compared with their thermal energy.
deeper: Solids have fixed positions, liquids flow while staying dense, gases fill containers, and plasmas are ionised gases. Phase diagrams map the conditions.
expert: Ideal gas PV=nRT; van der Waals (P+an²/V²)(V−nb)=nRT; water triple point 273.16 K, 611.657 Pa (see the phase diagram; the kelvin was defined by this point before 2019).
regime: Real behaviour near critical points departs from simple laws.

title: Composition and properties of air
basics: Dry air is about 78 % nitrogen, 21 % oxygen and about 1 % argon, with traces of carbon dioxide and other gases. In the real atmosphere pressure halves about every 5.5 km of altitude; an isothermal atmosphere with H≈8.5 km would give 5.9 km.
deeper: Water vapour varies up to a few percent. Oxygen is a by-product of photosynthesis and was almost absent before about 2.4 billion years ago.
expert: N₂ 78.08 %, O₂ 20.95 %, Ar 0.93 %; ρ_air=1.2 kg/m³ at 20 °C; scale height H=kT/mg≈8.5 km.
regime: Barometric law assumes isothermal atmosphere.
evidence: Direct gas analysis of dry air (NOAA/NIST composition measurements)

title: Solutions and colloids
basics: Substances dissolve when attractions to the solvent compensate for breaking their own bonds. Water's polarity dissolves salts and sugars but not oils.
deeper: Concentration is measured as molarity; dissolved particles change boiling, freezing and osmotic pressure. Colloids such as milk are mixtures where tiny droplets or particles stay dispersed without settling.
expert: M=n/V; Raoult P=xP°; Π=iMRT; ΔT_f=i K_f m (ideal dilute solutions; i is the van 't Hoff factor).
regime: Ideal solutions assumed; ionic solutions deviate.

title: Thermochemistry and enthalpy
basics: Chemical reactions absorb or release heat because bonds break and form. Enthalpy change measures the heat at constant pressure.
deeper: Hess's law lets you add reactions to find unknown enthalpies. Burning fuels releases energy because the products have stronger bonds.
expert: ΔH°_rxn=ΣΔH_f°(products)−ΣΔH_f°(reactants); CH₄(g)+2O₂(g)→CO₂(g)+2H₂O(l) ΔH°=−890 kJ/mol (−802 kJ/mol if H₂O is a gas); glucose combustion −2803 kJ/mol.
regime: Standard-state values at 298 K.

title: Gibbs free energy and spontaneity
basics: At constant temperature and pressure, a process happens on its own if it lowers the Gibbs free energy, which balances heat released against disorder gained. Free energy sets which reactions can run and how far.
deeper: Cells couple unfavourable reactions to ATP hydrolysis to drive them. Entropy matters most at high temperature.
expert: ΔG=ΔH−TΔS; ΔG°=−RT ln K; ATP hydrolysis ΔG°′≈−30.5 kJ/mol; ΔG=−nFE.
regime: Says whether a reaction can occur, not how fast.

title: Chemical equilibrium and acid-base
basics: Reactions run both ways until forward and reverse rates match. Acids donate protons and bases accept them, and pH measures acidity on a logarithmic scale.
deeper: Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium shifts to counter an imposed change. Buffers resist pH change, which is vital for blood (pH 7.4).
expert: K=[C]^c[D]^d/([A]^a[B]^b); pH=−log[H⁺]; pH=pKa+log([A⁻]/[HA]); K_w=10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
regime: Concentrations should be activities for non-dilute solutions.

title: Reaction kinetics and catalysis
basics: How fast a reaction goes depends on collisions with enough energy to cross an activation barrier. Catalysts and enzymes lower that barrier without being used up.
deeper: Rate rises sharply with temperature; a 10 °C rise often doubles it. Transition state theory links rates to energy landscapes.
expert: k=A e^{−E_a/RT}; rate=k[A]^m[B]^n; first-order t_{1/2}=ln2/k; Eyring k=(k_BT/h)e^{−ΔG‡/RT}.
regime: Rate laws must be measured; they are not read from stoichiometry.

title: Redox and electrochemistry
basics: Redox reactions move electrons from one species to another, and when the two halves are separated this produces an electric current. Batteries and corrosion are electrochemistry.
deeper: Standard potentials rank how readily substances gain electrons. Cell voltage depends on concentrations via the Nernst equation.
expert: ΔG=−nFE; E=E°−(RT/nF)lnQ; F=96485 C/mol; Li-ion cell ≈3.6–3.7 V.
regime: Equilibrium potentials; kinetics (overpotential) matter in devices.

title: Organic chemistry and functional groups
basics: Carbon can form four bonds and chains, so it supports millions of compounds. Groups of atoms such as alcohols, acids and amines decide a molecule's reactions.
deeper: Reaction mechanisms track electron pairs moving from nucleophile to electrophile. Chirality means a molecule and its mirror image can behave differently in living systems.
expert: sp³ C–C 154 pm, sp² C=C 134 pm, sp C≡C 120 pm; SN2 rate=k[RX][Nu]; benzene resonance ≈150 kJ/mol.
regime: Mechanisms are models consistent with kinetics and isotope tests.

title: Stereochemistry and chirality
basics: Many molecules exist as mirror images that cannot be superimposed. Biology uses almost only one hand: L-amino acids and D-sugars.
deeper: The two forms of a drug can have different effects. Why life chose one handedness is unresolved.
expert: R/S via Cahn-Ingold-Prelog; specific rotation [α]=α/(l·c); enantiomeric excess ee=|R−S|/(R+S).
regime: Chirality arises whenever a molecule cannot be superimposed on its mirror image, usually from a stereogenic centre but also from axes, planes or helices.
evidence: Thalidomide: the S-form binds cereblon and causes birth defects, but the two forms interconvert in the body, so a single-enantiomer drug would not have avoided the harm

title: Spectroscopy: how we identify molecules
basics: Molecules absorb specific energies of radio, infrared and visible light. NMR, IR and mass spectrometry reveal their structure and composition.
deeper: NMR uses nuclear spin in a magnetic field, the same physics as MRI. Mass spectrometry weighs ions.
expert: NMR ν=γB/2π (¹H: 42.58 MHz/T); IR C=O stretch ≈1650–1800 cm⁻¹ (ketone ≈1715); m/z=mass/charge.
regime: Needs reference data and sample prep.
evidence: X-ray structures checked against NMR/IR assignments

title: Polymers and plastics
basics: Polymers are long chains made of repeating units. Natural examples are DNA, proteins and cellulose; synthetic ones include polyethylene and nylon.
deeper: Chain length and cross-linking determine stiffness and melting. Most plastics persist because their long, water-repelling chains resist microbes and they degrade only slowly; a few enzymes that break PET and some polyesters have been found.
expert: M_n, M_w, PDI=M_w/M_n; polyethylene (–CH₂–)ₙ T_m≈135 °C (HDPE); Tg of PMMA ≈105 °C.
regime: T_m and T_g depend on chain structure and molar mass (HDPE ≈130–137 °C; atactic PMMA T_g ≈105 °C). Entangled-chain dynamics are described by reptation theory.

title: Transition metals and coordination chemistry
basics: Transition metals such as iron and copper bind molecules called ligands to form coloured, reactive complexes. Iron sits at the heart of haemoglobin and cytochromes, and copper in some oxygen carriers and electron-transfer proteins. (Chlorophyll uses magnesium.)
deeper: Crystal field theory explains the colour of many complexes through d-d transitions; charge-transfer bands explain others, such as permanganate. Metalloproteins use this chemistry to carry oxygen and transfer electrons.
expert: Δ_oct splitting: [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ ≈20 300 cm⁻¹ (blue-green absorption); 18-electron rule.
regime: Models are semi-quantitative; DFT used for accuracy.

title: Nitrogen fixation and Haber-Bosch
basics: Plants need fixed nitrogen, which is scarce because N₂ has a very strong triple bond. The Haber-Bosch process makes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen and feeds roughly half of humanity.
deeper: It runs at ~400–500 °C and 150–300 atm over an iron catalyst. Industrial fixation now rivals natural land fixation.
expert: N₂+3H₂⇌2NH₃, ΔH=−92 kJ/mol; N≡N 945 kJ/mol; global ammonia output ≈1.5×10⁸ t of nitrogen per year (≈1.8–1.9×10⁸ t as NH₃), recent USGS estimates.
regime: Energy-intensive; catalysts working at mild conditions are an active research target.

title: Computational chemistry (DFT, molecular dynamics)
basics: Computers approximate quantum mechanics to predict molecule shapes and reactions. Density functional theory handles hundreds of atoms; molecular dynamics follows thousands to millions with simpler forces.
deeper: Accuracy is good for ground-state organic chemistry but limited for strongly correlated systems like some transition-metal catalysts.
expert: E[ρ]=T_s+E_H+E_xc+∫Vρ; MD: m r̈=−∇U with Δt≈1–2 fs; chemical accuracy ≈1 kcal/mol (4.2 kJ/mol).
regime: Functional choice and sampling limits cap accuracy.

title: Crystals and lattices
basics: In crystals atoms sit in repeating three-dimensional patterns. There are 14 Bravais lattices and 230 space groups.
deeper: Crystal structure controls hardness, cleavage, optical and electronic properties. X-ray diffraction reveals the arrangement.
expert: Bragg: 2d sinθ=nλ; fcc packing fraction 0.74; Si lattice a=0.543 nm; NaCl a=0.564 nm.
regime: Real crystals contain defects.

title: Band theory of solids
basics: In solids, electron energy levels merge into bands with gaps between them. Whether the top band is full or has a gap decides if a material is a metal, insulator or semiconductor.
deeper: Metals conduct because electrons can easily move to nearby levels. Semiconductors have gaps of about 1 eV that can be crossed by heat or light and adjusted by doping.
expert: E(k) bands; E_g(Si)=1.12 eV, E_g(GaAs)=1.42 eV, diamond 5.5 eV; Fermi level; σ=neμ.
regime: Independent-electron picture; strong correlations break it (Mott insulators).

title: Semiconductors, p-n junctions and transistors
basics: Adding small amounts of impurities makes a semiconductor carry current with electrons (n-type) or holes (p-type). Joining them makes a diode. A bipolar transistor has three layers; the MOSFET used in processors has a gate controlling a channel between source and drain.
deeper: A transistor is a switch with a gate that controls the current. Billions of them form a processor.
expert: Shockley diode I=I_s(e^{V/V_T}−1), V_T=kT/q≈25.9 mV at 300 K (25.7 mV at 298 K); MOSFET threshold V_th≈0.3–1 V; modern gate pitch ~tens of nm.
regime: Quantum tunnelling and heat limit further miniaturisation.

title: Superconductivity
basics: Below a critical temperature some materials conduct electricity with zero resistance and expel magnetic fields. Electrons pair up and move together.
deeper: In conventional superconductors the pairing is mediated by lattice vibrations (BCS theory). High-temperature copper-oxide superconductors work above liquid-nitrogen temperature but their mechanism is not settled.
expert: BCS gap Δ≈1.76 k_BT_c; Nb T_c=9.2 K, YBa₂Cu₃O₇ T_c≈92 K; London depth λ_L=√(m/μ₀ne²).
regime: Room-temperature ambient-pressure superconductivity has not been verified; the 2023 LK-99 claim failed replication.

title: Magnetic materials
basics: Iron, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic because the exchange interaction aligns neighbouring electron spins; the material then splits into domains to lower its magnetic field energy. Heating above the Curie temperature destroys the order.
deeper: Hard drives store bits in magnetic domains. Magnetic order is a classic example of spontaneous symmetry breaking.
expert: Curie T_c(Fe)=1043 K; μ_B=9.274×10⁻²⁴ J/T; above T_c, Curie-Weiss χ=C/(T−T_c), with C the Curie constant.
regime: Exchange interaction is quantum mechanical in origin.

title: Defects, dislocations and material strength
basics: Real metals are far weaker than perfect crystals because lines of misplaced atoms (dislocations) slide easily. Making them harder to move strengthens the metal.
deeper: Alloying, work hardening and fine grains block dislocations. Steel's strength is tuned by carbon content and heat treatment.
expert: τ_theory≈G/10–G/30; τ_real≈G/10²–10⁵, from strong alloys to pure single crystals; Hall-Petch σ_y=σ₀+k d^{−1/2}; steel yield ≈250–1500 MPa.
regime: Hall-Petch holds down to grain sizes of ~10–20 nm; below that, strength may fall. Brittle ceramics fail by cracks instead (Griffith criterion).

title: Metals, ceramics, composites and glass
basics: Engineers choose materials by linking structure to properties: metals are tough and conductive, ceramics hard and heat-resistant, polymers light, composites combine strengths, and glass is an amorphous solid with a liquid-like atomic arrangement.
deeper: Carbon-fibre composites have about one fifth the density of steel and, along the fibres, comparable or higher strength. Glass has no long-range order, so it lacks sharp melting.
expert: Density: Al 2.70, steel 7.85, CFRP ~1.6 g/cm³; E: diamond 1050 GPa, glass 70 GPa.
regime: Properties depend on processing as well as composition.

title: Soft matter and liquid crystals
basics: Gels, foams, colloids, polymers and liquid crystals are soft because thermal motion is comparable to their binding energy. Cells are largely soft matter.
deeper: Liquid crystals let screens switch light with small voltages. Self-assembly of lipids into bilayers is a soft-matter process.
expert: Entropic spring F=3k_BT x/(N b²); persistence length DNA ≈50 nm; Brownian D=k_BT/6πηr.
regime: No single unifying theory.

frontier.text: Is there a general theory of glassy dynamics and jamming?

title: Topological phases and 2D materials
basics: Some materials have conduction that is protected by the global shape of their electron states. Quantum-Hall systems are the classic example. Graphene, one atom-thick carbon, is the best-known 2D material and shows the quantum Hall effect, though by itself it is not a topological insulator.
deeper: Quantum-Hall resistance is quantised to extreme precision, now used in electrical standards. Twisted layers (moiré materials) show correlated and superconducting phases.
expert: R_H=h/(νe²), h/e²=25 812.807 Ω; graphene mobility up to ~10⁵ cm²/V s at room temperature in clean encapsulated samples (≈10⁴ on SiO₂).
regime: Active research; practical devices still emerging.

frontier.text: Strange metals and moiré physics poorly understood

title: Photovoltaics (solar cells)
basics: A solar cell is a p-n junction that turns absorbed photons into electric current. Silicon cells convert roughly 20–25 % of sunlight.
deeper: The Shockley-Queisser limit is about 33 % at the best band gap and about 29 % for silicon; the best silicon cells reach ~27 %. Perovskites and tandem cells are research frontiers, with stability a main hurdle.
expert: SQ limit ≈33 % at E_g≈1.34 eV; Si record ≈26–27 %; P_sun at Earth 1361 W/m² (about 1000 W/m² at the surface under clear sky at the AM1.5 standard test condition).
regime: Multijunction cells exceed single-junction limit.

title: The four classes of biomolecules
basics: Life is built from carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids, all made largely of carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur.
deeper: Carbohydrates, proteins and nucleic acids are polymers of sugars, amino acids and nucleotides. Lipids are different: they are built from fatty acids and other small parts but are not chains of repeating units, and they are grouped by their water-avoiding character. Their shapes and charges decide what they do.
expert: CHONPS ≈ 97–98 % of body mass; ~20 amino acids, 4 DNA bases; glucose C₆H₁₂O₆ (180 g/mol); average amino-acid residue ≈110 Da.
regime: Living things also need trace elements such as Fe, Zn, Mg, Mo and Se; which ones vary by organism, but Fe, Zn and Mg are used almost universally.

title: Carbohydrates and lipids
basics: Sugars store quick energy and build structures like cellulose; fats (triglycerides) store much more energy per gram, and phospholipids, a related lipid, form cell membranes.
deeper: Glucose chains make starch (plant storage), glycogen (animal storage) and cellulose (plant walls). Fatty acids have long hydrocarbon tails that avoid water.
expert: Fat ≈37 kJ/g vs carbohydrate ≈17 kJ/g; cellulose β-1,4 linkage; palmitic acid C₁₆H₃₂O₂.
regime: Digestibility depends on enzymes present (e.g. cellulase absent in humans).

title: Proteins: structure and folding
basics: A protein is a chain of amino acids that folds into a specific 3D shape set by its sequence. The shape allows it to act as an enzyme, motor, channel or building block.
deeper: Four levels: sequence, local helices and sheets, overall fold and multi-chain assemblies. Folding is driven by hiding oily groups and forming hydrogen bonds. Many proteins also have flexible disordered regions.
expert: Peptide bond 0.133 nm; α-helix 3.6 residues/turn, 0.54 nm pitch; Levinthal paradox: a ~150-residue chain has ~10³⁰⁰ possible conformations yet folds in ms–s; ΔG_fold≈−20 to −60 kJ/mol.
regime: Prediction of static folds is now accurate; dynamics and design remain challenging.

frontier.text: Full dynamics of folding and multi-conformation states

title: Enzymes and catalysis in cells
basics: Enzymes are mostly protein catalysts (some are RNA) that speed up reactions by factors of a million or far more, chiefly by stabilising the transition state. Each acts on specific substrates.
deeper: Michaelis-Menten kinetics describes how rate saturates with substrate. Inhibitors and allosteric regulators tune enzymes.
expert: v=V_max[S]/(K_m+[S]); k_cat/K_m up to ~10⁸–10⁹ M⁻¹s⁻¹ (diffusion limit); catalase k_cat≈10⁷ s⁻¹.
regime: Idealised for single substrate steady state.

title: ATP: the cell's energy currency
basics: ATP is an unstable, far-from-equilibrium molecule: when it is hydrolysed to ADP and phosphate the products are much more stable, and that drop in free energy is what cells couple to other reactions. The energy is not held in a single bond. Cells use this to power movement, building and pumping, then rebuild ATP from food or light.
deeper: A human recycles roughly their own body weight in ATP every day. Many reactions are coupled to ATP hydrolysis.
expert: ATP+H₂O→ADP+Pi, ΔG°′≈−30.5 kJ/mol (≈−50 kJ/mol in cells); ~10²¹ ATP molecules/s used by a human at rest.
regime: Used by nearly all life; other nucleotides (GTP) also carry energy.

title: Metabolism: glycolysis, Krebs cycle and respiration
basics: Cells extract energy from glucose in stages: glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor in humans.
deeper: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP in the cytoplasm; pyruvate oxidation, the Krebs cycle and electron transport in the mitochondrion bring the total to about 30–32 ATP per glucose.
expert: C₆H₁₂O₆+6O₂→6CO₂+6H₂O, ΔG°′=−2870 kJ/mol; ~30–32 ATP per glucose; fermentation 2 ATP.
regime: Yield varies with proton leak and tissue.

title: Chemiosmosis and ATP synthase
basics: Electrons from food pass along protein complexes in the mitochondrial membrane, pumping protons across it. The proton flow back through ATP synthase, a tiny rotary motor, makes ATP.
deeper: Peter Mitchell's chemiosmotic idea unites respiration and photosynthesis. The enzyme rotates about 100 times per second.
expert: Proton motive force Δp=Δψ−(2.3RT/F)ΔpH ≈ 150–200 mV; ~3–4 H⁺ per ATP; F₁F₀ rotates ~100–150 Hz.
regime: Common to mitochondria, chloroplasts and bacteria.

title: Photosynthesis
basics: Plants, algae and some bacteria capture sunlight to turn CO₂ and water into sugar and oxygen. This process supplies food and the oxygen in air.
deeper: The light reactions use chlorophyll to split water and make ATP and NADPH; the Calvin cycle uses them to fix carbon with the enzyme Rubisco.
expert: 6CO₂+6H₂O+photons→C₆H₁₂O₆+6O₂; ΔG°′≈+2870 kJ/mol; theoretical max conversion ≈4.6 % for C₃ plants; photons 400–700 nm.
regime: Rubisco also reacts with O₂ (photorespiration), lowering efficiency.

title: DNA structure and replication
basics: DNA is a double helix of two strands, with the bases A-T and G-C pairing across the middle. Its sequence stores genetic information and it is copied before cells divide.
deeper: Each strand serves as a template for a new partner (semi-conservative replication), carried out by DNA polymerase, whose proofreading brings errors to about 1 per 10⁷ bases; mismatch repair then cuts this to about 1 per 10⁹–10¹⁰.
expert: Helix diameter 2.0 nm, 0.34 nm per base pair, 10.5 bp per turn; human genome ≈3.1×10⁹ bp per haploid set (≈6.2×10⁹ bp in a diploid cell), which at 0.34 nm per bp is ≈2 m of DNA per cell; final error rate ≈10⁻⁹–10⁻¹⁰ after proofreading and mismatch repair.
regime: Universal in cellular life; some viruses use RNA genomes.

title: Central dogma: transcription and translation
basics: DNA is copied into RNA, and RNA is read by ribosomes to build proteins. A three-letter genetic code in RNA specifies each amino acid.
deeper: The code has 64 codons for 20 amino acids and stop signals, nearly universal. Exceptions exist. Retroviruses such as HIV reverse the direction using reverse transcriptase (RNA→DNA), and most other RNA viruses copy RNA directly with an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
expert: 64 codons→20 aa+3 stops; AUG start; ribosome adds ≈15–20 aa/s (bacteria); RNA polymerase ≈50 nt/s.
regime: Near-universal code with documented variants.

title: Gene regulation and epigenetics
basics: Cells with the same DNA become different types by switching genes on and off. Proteins bind DNA near genes, and chemical tags on DNA and histones adjust accessibility.
deeper: Bacteria regulate genes by operons like lac; animals use enhancers and chromatin states. Epigenetic marks can be inherited through cell division.
expert: Lac operon induction by allolactose; DNA methylation at CpG; ~1,600 human transcription factors; enhancer-promoter loops 10⁴–10⁶ bp.
regime: Transgenerational epigenetic inheritance in humans is not established.

title: Chromatin, chromosomes and the genome
basics: DNA is wrapped around protein spools (nucleosomes) and folded into chromosomes. Humans have 46 chromosomes holding about 20,000 protein-coding genes.
deeper: Only about 1–2 % of the genome codes for protein; the rest includes regulatory regions, repeats and RNA genes. The first gap-free sequence of a human genome (CHM13, without a Y chromosome) was published in 2022, and a complete Y chromosome followed in 2023.
expert: Nucleosome: 147 bp around 8 histones; 3.1 Gbp; ≈20 000 protein-coding genes; mitochondrial genome 16.6 kb.
regime: Function of much non-coding DNA is still being mapped.

title: CRISPR and genetic engineering
basics: CRISPR is a bacterial immune system adapted as a tool to edit DNA at chosen sites. It is used in research, agriculture and the first approved gene-editing therapy.
deeper: A guide RNA directs the Cas9 enzyme to a matching DNA sequence and cuts it, after which cells repair the cut. Careful design limits off-target edits.
expert: 20-nt guide RNA; PAM NGG for SpCas9; edit efficiencies vary 10–90 %.
regime: Off-target effects and delivery limit therapies.

title: Cell membranes and lipid bilayers
basics: A cell is wrapped in a two-layer sheet of lipids whose water-loving heads face outside and oily tails face inward. This barrier keeps the cell's contents separate.
deeper: Proteins embedded in the bilayer act as channels, pumps and receptors. The membrane is fluid, with lipids and proteins drifting sideways.
expert: Bilayer thickness ≈4–5 nm; lateral D≈10⁻¹² m²/s for lipids; membrane potential ≈−70 mV in neurons.
regime: Fluid mosaic model; lipid rafts remain debated.

title: Membrane transport and osmosis
basics: Small nonpolar gases cross membranes easily; water crosses slowly through the lipid itself and much faster through aquaporin channels, while ions and large molecules need channels or pumps. Water moves toward higher solute concentration by osmosis.
deeper: Pumps like the sodium-potassium ATPase spend ATP to build gradients, which cells then use for signals, nutrient uptake and ATP production.
expert: Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in per ATP; osmotic Π=iMRT; aquaporin ≈3×10⁹ water/s per channel.
regime: Passive diffusion follows concentration gradients (the electrochemical gradient for ions); active transport requires energy.

title: Cells: the unit of life
basics: All living things are made of cells, cells come from other cells, and a cell is the smallest unit that can live on its own. Cells range from bacteria to neurons.
deeper: Prokaryotic cells lack a nucleus; eukaryotic cells contain organelles. Cells keep their internal chemistry different from outside by controlling what crosses the membrane.
expert: Bacterium 1–5 μm, animal cell 10–30 μm, human egg ≈100 μm; ≈3×10¹³ human cells (reference adult; older estimates ≈3.7×10¹³).
regime: Viruses are not cells.

title: Organelles: nucleus, ER, Golgi, lysosomes
basics: Eukaryotic cells divide work among compartments: the nucleus stores DNA, the ER and Golgi build and ship proteins, and lysosomes recycle waste.
deeper: Proteins are labelled with signal sequences that route them to the right place. Vesicles carry cargo between compartments.
expert: Nucleus ≈6 μm; nuclear pore ≈120 MDa complex; ribosomes ≈20 nm (bacteria) to ≈25–30 nm (eukaryotes); lysosome pH≈4.5–5.
regime: Details differ among kingdoms.

title: Mitochondria and endosymbiosis
basics: Mitochondria are the cell's power plants and descend from bacteria that took up residence in an ancestor of all complex cells about 2 billion years ago. Chloroplasts arose similarly from cyanobacteria.
deeper: They have their own small DNA and ribosomes. The origin of the host cell is debated, with archaea from the Asgard group as leading candidates.
expert: Mitochondrion ≈1–2 μm; mtDNA 16.6 kb (37 genes); ≈10³ per cell; cristae increase surface area for ATP synthase.
regime: Endosymbiosis itself is settled; host identity debated.

frontier.text: Details of eukaryogenesis from archaea plus bacterium

title: Chloroplasts and plant cells
