basics: Chloroplasts are green organelles where photosynthesis happens. Plant cells also have rigid cellulose walls and a large water-filled vacuole.
deeper: Stacks of membranes called thylakoids hold chlorophyll and the electron-transport machinery. Turgor pressure from the vacuole keeps soft plants upright.
expert: Chloroplast 4–10 μm; ≈30–120 per leaf mesophyll cell depending on species; chlorophyll absorbs ≈430 and 662 nm; turgor 0.3–1 MPa.
regime: Found in plants and algae (and a few other eukaryotes by secondary endosymbiosis); the cellulose wall and large central vacuole are features of plant cells.

title: Cell division: mitosis and meiosis
basics: Cells copy their DNA and split into two identical daughters by mitosis. Meiosis halves the chromosome number to make eggs and sperm and shuffles genes.
deeper: Checkpoint proteins stop division if DNA is damaged. Loss of these controls is a hallmark of cancer.
expert: Human cell cycle ≈24 h in fast-dividing cultured cells; M phase ≈1 h; meiosis I recombination ≈1–3 crossovers per chromosome pair (≈30–50 per human meiosis, more in females than males).
regime: Bacteria divide by binary fission.

title: Cell signalling and apoptosis
basics: Cells communicate using chemical messengers that bind receptors, triggering relay chains inside the cell. Cells can also self-destruct (apoptosis) when damaged or no longer needed.
deeper: Hormones, growth factors and neurotransmitters use different receptor types. Apoptosis shapes fingers in development and removes damaged cells.
expert: G-protein-coupled receptors ≈800 in humans; cAMP second messenger; caspase cascade.
regime: Cross-talk makes pathways networks not lines.

title: Cytoskeleton and molecular motors
basics: A network of protein filaments gives cells shape and acts as tracks for motor proteins, which carry cargo and make muscles contract.
deeper: Kinesin walks along microtubules in 8-nanometre steps, burning one ATP per step.
expert: Microtubule diameter 25 nm; actin 7 nm; kinesin step 8 nm, force ≈6 pN, speed ≈0.8 μm/s; myosin step ≈5–10 nm.
regime: Dynamics regulated by many accessory proteins.

title: Viruses
basics: Viruses are packages of genetic material in a protein shell that reproduce only inside host cells. They are not cells and carry no metabolism of their own.
deeper: They hijack the cell's machinery to make copies. Vaccines train immunity against viral proteins; antivirals target specific viral enzymes.
expert: SARS-CoV-2 ≈100 nm, 30 kb RNA; T4 phage ≈200 nm, 169 kb DNA; ΦX174 5.4 kb; mutation rates RNA ≈10⁻⁴–10⁻⁶/nt.
regime: Their classification as 'alive' is a definitional debate.

title: Bacteria, archaea and microbes
basics: Microbes are the most abundant and diverse life, living from deep rocks to our guts. Bacteria and archaea are single-celled without a nucleus, and microbes drive Earth's chemical cycles.
deeper: Bacteria can swap genes sideways (conjugation, transformation). The gut microbiome affects digestion, but many claimed links to disease are still correlations.
expert: ≈10³⁰ prokaryote cells on Earth; E. coli doubling ≈20 min, genome 4.6 Mb; human body ≈4×10¹³ bacteria (mostly in the colon), about the same as the number of human cells.
regime: Causal health effects of microbiome remain C3.

frontier.text: Causal roles of the microbiome in disease

title: Mendelian and molecular inheritance
basics: Traits pass from parents to offspring in discrete units (genes). Each parent gives one copy; dominant versions mask recessive ones.
deeper: Linked genes, sex chromosomes and mutations extend Mendel's rules. Most traits are polygenic, shaped by many genes and the environment.
expert: Monohybrid cross 3:1, dihybrid 9:3:3:1; Hardy-Weinberg p²+2pq+q²=1; human mutation rate ≈1.2×10⁻⁸ per bp per generation.
regime: Polygenic traits follow quantitative-genetic models.

title: Evolution by natural selection
basics: Individuals vary, some variants leave more offspring, and traits that are heritable accumulate over generations. This process explains the adaptation and diversity of life.
deeper: Other forces matter too: mutation, genetic drift, gene flow and sexual selection. Observed evolution includes antibiotic resistance and the Lenski long-term E. coli experiment.
expert: Breeder's equation R=h²S; selection coefficient s; fixation probability ≈2s for new beneficial mutation; Δp=sp(1−p).
regime: Applies wherever there is variation, heredity and differential reproduction.

title: Common descent and phylogenetics
basics: All living things share a single family tree. DNA similarity, anatomy and fossils show how species are related.
deeper: Molecular clocks use mutation counts to date branch points. Nearly universal genetic code and shared genes point to a common ancestor.
expert: Human-chimp genome ≈98.8 % similar (SNPs); split ≈6–7 Ma; molecular clock d=2μt.
regime: Horizontal gene transfer blurs the tree among microbes.

title: Speciation and the diversity of life
basics: New species form when populations are isolated and diverge. About two million species are described, and the true number is far higher.
deeper: Estimates of total species range from several million to much larger numbers if microbes are included. Mass extinctions have repeatedly reset diversity.
expert: ~2.2 million described eukaryote species; ≈8.7 M eukaryotes estimated (2011); five mass extinctions.
regime: Total species count estimates remain uncertain.

title: Mass extinctions and major transitions
basics: Life's history has major transitions (eukaryotes, multicellularity, land) and five mass extinctions. The last, 66 million years ago, wiped out non-avian dinosaurs after an asteroid impact.
deeper: The end-Permian extinction ~252 Ma was the worst, linked to volcanism. The Cambrian explosion ~540 Ma saw most animal body plans appear.
expert: Chicxulub impactor ≈10 km, crater ≈180 km; Permian loss ≈80–95 % marine species; K-Pg boundary iridium anomaly.
regime: Causes of some events debated.
evidence: Schulte et al. 2010, Science (Chicxulub impact and the end-Cretaceous extinction)

title: Human evolution
basics: Humans share ancestors with chimpanzees from ~6–7 million years ago. Homo sapiens arose in Africa and interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans.
deeper: Bipedalism came first, large brains later. Ancient DNA shows that non-African people carry ≈1–2 % Neanderthal ancestry.
expert: H. sapiens ≈300 ka; brain volume ≈1350 cm³; Neanderthal DNA ≈1–2 % in non-Africans.
regime: Dates revised as new fossils and DNA appear.

title: Origin of life
basics: How non-living chemistry became living cells is still unknown. Leading ideas include RNA-first replication, hydrothermal vents, and wet-dry pools on land.
deeper: Experiments make amino acids, sugars and nucleotides from simple starting molecules, and some RNAs act as catalysts. A step from chemistry to self-replicating cells has not been reproduced.
expert: Miller-Urey 1953 produced amino acids; ribozyme polymerases extend ≈100+ nt; protocell vesicle size ≈1 μm.
regime: No consensus; any scenario must fit early-Earth geochemistry.

frontier.text: Start of replication and the genetic code

title: RNA world hypothesis
basics: RNA can both store information and catalyse reactions, so it may have preceded DNA and proteins. The ribosome's core is made of RNA, a clue.
deeper: It leaves open how RNA first formed and how the shift to DNA and proteins occurred.
expert: Hammerhead and RNase P ribozymes; peptidyl transferase is rRNA; non-enzymatic copying of RNA templates is slow and error-prone (errors of order a few percent per nucleotide in typical experiments), far below what is needed to maintain long genomes.
regime: Plausible stage, not a proven origin.

frontier.text: How the first RNAs formed from prebiotic chemistry (the ribonucleotide synthesis and polymerisation problem)
Whether RNA came first or alongside peptides, lipids and metabolism

title: Last universal common ancestor (LUCA)
basics: All present life descends from one ancestral population, the last universal common ancestor, which lived billions of years ago.
deeper: Shared genes across bacteria and archaea hint at what LUCA needed, but its age and lifestyle are estimated indirectly.
expert: Molecular-clock estimates place LUCA around 4.2 Ga (a 2024 study; uncertainty several hundred Myr), with a few hundred universal gene families; disputed microfossil and stromatolite evidence for life reaches back ≈3.5 Ga.
regime: Dates depend on molecular-clock calibration.

frontier.text: Age and lifestyle of LUCA (4.2 Ga estimate vs younger and older proposals)
Whether LUCA was a single organism or a community exchanging genes

title: Tissues and cell differentiation
basics: Humans have about 200 classically named cell types (the Human Cell Atlas has already told apart more than 500, and the true number is still being worked out), arranged in four tissue kinds: epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous. They differ mostly in which genes are active, not in their DNA (exceptions include lymphocytes, whose receptor genes are rearranged, and red blood cells, which lose their nucleus).
deeper: Stem cells can renew themselves and give rise to specialised cells. Induced pluripotent stem cells show that adult cells can be reprogrammed.
expert: ≈30×10¹² cells in a human (Sender et al. 2016; older estimates ≈37×10¹²); iPSC via Oct4, Sox2, Klf4, c-Myc (Yamanaka 2006).
regime: Cell-type counts depend on the classification scheme.

title: Embryonic development
basics: A fertilised egg divides and organises into a body through gradients of signalling molecules. Hox genes mark positions along the head-to-tail axis.
deeper: Cells decide fates by reading morphogen concentrations and neighbours. Regeneration and organoid research try to reuse these programmes.
expert: Human gestation ≈266 days; ≈45 rounds of cell doubling (≈3×10¹³ cell divisions in total, more counting cells that die) to build ≈3×10¹³ cells; Bicoid gradient length ≈100 μm in fly embryo; Turing reaction-diffusion patterns.
regime: How genomes encode 3D form is incompletely understood.

frontier.text: How genome-encoded gene networks and mechanical forces together produce reproducible 3D organ shape

title: Ageing
basics: Bodies gradually lose function as damage accumulates and repair slows. Hallmarks include DNA damage, shortened telomeres and worn-out cells.
deeper: Calorie restriction extends lifespan in many animals, and some drugs lengthen it in mice. Applying this to humans is unproven.
expert: Telomere loss ≈50–100 bp per division; Hayflick limit ≈50 divisions; longest verified human lifespan 122 y 164 d (J. Calment, died 1997); whether a biological limit exists is debated.
regime: Mechanistic theories compete.

frontier.text: Mechanisms and modifiability of human ageing

title: Homeostasis and the human body plan
basics: Body systems cooperate to keep temperature, blood sugar and acidity near set points using negative feedback. Examples include shivering, sweating and insulin release.
deeper: Hormones and nerves act as sensors, controllers and effectors. Failure of these loops leads to diseases like diabetes.
expert: Core temp ≈36.5–37.5 °C (the old 37 °C is a convention); blood glucose ≈5 mmol/L fasting; blood pH 7.35–7.45; HR ≈70 bpm.
regime: Set points shift with age, circadian rhythm and stress.

title: Heart and circulation
basics: The heart pumps blood through arteries, tiny capillaries and veins, delivering oxygen and removing wastes. It beats about 100,000 times a day.
deeper: Pressure from the left ventricle drives flow; valves keep it one way. The heart's electrical pacemaker is the sinoatrial node.
expert: Cardiac output ≈5 L/min at rest, stroke volume ≈70 mL; BP 120/80 mmHg; capillary diameter ≈8 μm; aorta ≈2.5 cm.
regime: Poiseuille's law Q=πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL) assumes steady, laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid in a rigid straight tube; it is only an approximation in the pulsatile, elastic large arteries and when red cells are comparable to vessel size (capillaries).

title: Lungs and gas exchange
basics: Lungs bring oxygen into the blood and remove carbon dioxide across thin membranes of about 500 million tiny air sacs. Haemoglobin carries oxygen.
deeper: Breathing is driven by the diaphragm creating lower pressure in the chest. Gas moves across by diffusion.
expert: Alveolar area ≈70 m²; membrane thickness ≈0.5 μm; tidal volume ≈0.5 L; 12–16 breaths/min; SaO₂ ≈97–99 %.
regime: Altitude reduces partial pressure of O₂.

title: Haemoglobin and oxygen transport
basics: Haemoglobin in red blood cells holds iron-containing heme groups that bind oxygen in the lungs and release it in tissues. Carbon monoxide binds more strongly and is poisonous.
deeper: The four subunits bind oxygen cooperatively, giving an S-shaped saturation curve that suits loading and unloading.
expert: Hb: 4 subunits, 4 heme-Fe; ≈1.34 mL O₂/g Hb; P₅₀≈26 mmHg; Hill n≈2.8; red cell ≈7 μm.
regime: Shifts with pH, CO₂ and 2,3-BPG.

title: Digestion and kidneys
basics: The gut breaks food into small molecules with enzymes and acid, and the kidneys filter blood to remove wastes and regulate water and salts.
deeper: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons. The large intestine and microbes recover water and make some vitamins.
expert: Gut length ≈7–9 m; stomach pH 1.5–3.5; GFR ≈125 mL/min; ≈180 L filtered, 1.5 L urine per day.
regime: Digestive times vary with diet.

title: Hormones and the endocrine system
basics: Glands release hormones into the blood to coordinate growth, metabolism, stress and reproduction. Insulin and glucagon keep blood sugar steady.
deeper: Hormones act on receptors on or inside target cells. The hypothalamus and pituitary form the control centre.
expert: Insulin 5.8 kDa; cortisol peaks near waking; thyroxine regulates basal metabolic rate; feedback loops τ from minutes to days.
regime: Many interactions between hormones.

title: Bones, joints and muscle
basics: Bones form a rigid lever system, and muscles pull on them to move the body. Bone is a living composite of mineral and collagen that remodels under load.
deeper: Muscles are built of bundles of fibres that shorten when actin and myosin filaments slide past each other, driven by ATP and triggered by calcium.
expert: 206 bones; femur bears several times body weight; sarcomere ≈2.5 μm; muscle stress ≈0.3 MPa.
regime: Bone density declines with age.

title: Muscle contraction
basics: Muscle shortens when myosin heads grip actin filaments and pull, powered by ATP. A nerve signal releases calcium, which unlocks the filaments.
deeper: Each myosin head cycle moves actin about 5–10 nm. A head completes about 5–50 cycles per second, and a fibre contains billions of heads working out of step.
expert: Sarcomere shortening ≈ 1 μm; force per myosin head ≈3–5 pN; Ca²⁺ ≈10⁻⁷→10⁻⁵ M triggers contraction.
regime: Cross-bridge model; details of power stroke debated.

title: Skin and the body's barrier
basics: Skin is the body's largest organ, forming a waterproof barrier that regulates temperature and senses touch. Its outer layer is made of dead keratin-filled cells that constantly shed.
deeper: Melanin absorbs UV; sweat glands cool by evaporation. Skin renews roughly every month.
expert: Area ≈1.7–2 m²; epidermis thickness 0.05–1.5 mm; sweat evaporation ≈2.4 MJ/kg.
regime: Thickness and pigment vary across body and individuals.

title: Immune system: innate and adaptive
basics: The immune system defends against pathogens with barriers, fast generic responses (innate) and slower learned ones (adaptive) that remember past infections.
deeper: B cells make antibodies and T cells coordinate or kill infected cells. Gene shuffling creates an enormous variety of receptors.
expert: V(D)J recombination ≈10¹¹–10¹⁵ possible receptors; antibody ≈150 kDa; fever ≈38–39 °C; memory lasts years to decades.
regime: Autoimmunity and allergy are failures of discrimination.

title: Germ theory, vaccines and antibiotics
basics: Infectious diseases are caused by microbes. Sanitation, vaccines and antibiotics have produced the largest gains in life expectancy in history.
deeper: Vaccines prime memory immunity without disease; antibiotics kill bacteria or stop their growth. Resistance evolves by natural selection.
expert: Smallpox eradicated 1980; penicillin 1928/1940s; R₀ measles ≈12–18; herd immunity threshold 1−1/R₀.
regime: Antibiotic resistance erodes treatments. Herd immunity threshold 1−1/R₀ (homogeneous mixing, fully effective vaccine; with efficacy E the needed coverage is (1−1/R₀)/E).

title: Pharmacology and drug action
basics: Most drugs work by binding to specific proteins like receptors or enzymes and altering their activity. Dose determines effect and side effects.
deeper: Drug development moves from molecule discovery to randomised controlled trials, the gold standard for showing a treatment works.
expert: Dose-response E=E_max C/(EC₅₀+C); half-life t_{1/2}=0.693V_d/CL; IC₅₀ nM–μM; aspirin inhibits COX.
regime: Individual response varies with genes and other drugs.

title: Cancer
basics: Cancer arises when accumulated mutations let cells ignore growth controls and spread. It is many diseases, not one.
deeper: Mutations in oncogenes and tumour-suppressor genes such as p53 combine over years. Immunotherapy releases immune cells against tumours.
expert: Typically 2–8 driver mutations; ≈10⁹ cells in a 1 cm³ (≈1 g) tumour; a tumour first detectable on a scan already holds about this many; p53 mutated in ≈50 % of cancers.
regime: Risk rises steeply with age.

title: Medical imaging
basics: X-rays, CT, MRI, ultrasound and PET let doctors see inside the body. Each uses a different physical interaction: absorption, nuclear spin, echoes or positron annihilation.
deeper: MRI uses strong magnets and radio pulses on hydrogen nuclei in water; PET uses antimatter, since positrons annihilate with electrons.
expert: MRI Larmor f=42.58 MHz/T (1.5–3 T); X-ray 20–150 keV; ultrasound 2–15 MHz; PET γ=511 keV.
regime: X-ray, CT and PET use ionising radiation with dose limits; MRI and ultrasound do not, but have their own safety limits (implants, heating).

title: Magnetic resonance imaging
basics: MRI aligns the spins of hydrogen nuclei with a strong magnetic field, nudges them with radio pulses, and listens to the signals they emit as they relax.
deeper: Superconducting magnets give the field. Contrast comes from differences in how fast different tissues relax.
expert: ω_L=γB₀, γ/2π=42.58 MHz/T; at 1.5 T: T₁≈0.25–0.5 s for fat, ≈0.6–1.0 s for white and grey matter, ≈4 s for CSF, longer at higher field; T₂≈40–100 ms in most soft tissue.
regime: Contraindicated with some metal implants.

title: Neurons and action potentials
basics: Neurons send electrical pulses called action potentials along their fibres. The pulse is produced by sodium and potassium ions flowing through channels in the membrane.
deeper: The Hodgkin-Huxley model describes how voltage-gated channels open and close in sequence. Signals jump between myelin gaps to travel faster.
expert: Resting V≈−70 mV; threshold ≈−55 mV; peak ≈+40 mV; conduction 1–120 m/s; C_m≈1 μF/cm²; C dV/dt=−Σg_i(V−E_i).
regime: Stochastic channel opening adds noise.

title: Synapses and plasticity
basics: At a synapse one neuron releases chemicals (neurotransmitters) that excite or inhibit the next. Changing synapse strength with use is how brains learn.
deeper: Long-term potentiation strengthens synapses after repeated activity. Dopamine, serotonin and others modulate circuits.
expert: Synaptic cleft ≈20 nm; vesicle ≈40 nm, ≈5,000 molecules ACh; ≈10¹⁴ synapses in a human brain; delay ≈0.5 ms.
regime: Mechanisms of memory storage across timescales are still debated.

title: The brain: structure and function
basics: The human brain has about 86 billion neurons organised into regions for senses, movement, memory and reasoning. The cerebral cortex handles many higher functions.
deeper: Brain regions specialise but work in networks. Imaging methods like fMRI show where activity changes, not the precise neural code.
expert: 86×10⁹ neurons, ≈10¹⁴ synapses, mass ≈1.4 kg, power ≈20 W (≈20 % of body); cortex ≈2.5 mm thick.
regime: Localisation of function is approximate.

title: Connectomics and neural wiring
basics: Connectomics maps every neuron and synapse in a brain using electron microscopy. Complete maps exist for small animals and growing parts of mammal brains.
deeper: Wiring maps provide constraints for circuit models, but they do not give the strengths, chemistry or dynamics by themselves.
expert: C. elegans: 302 neurons, ≈7,000 synapses; adult Drosophila brain (FlyWire) ≈1.4×10⁵ neurons and ≈5×10⁷ synapses; MICrONS mouse cortex 1 mm³ ≈7×10⁴ neurons (≈2×10⁵ cells) and ≈5×10⁸ synapses.
regime: Structure alone does not determine function.

title: Senses: vision, hearing, touch, taste and smell
basics: Sensory cells convert physical signals (light, pressure waves, molecules) into electrical signals the brain interprets.
deeper: The retina has about 92 million rods and 4.6 million cones (Curcio et al. 1990, eight retinas; individuals vary by about 15 %); hair cells in the cochlea sense vibrations; olfactory receptors detect molecules.
expert: Human vision 380–750 nm; hearing 20 Hz–20 kHz; ≈400 olfactory receptor genes; a rod can respond to a single photon.
regime: Perception is a constructive process, not a recording.

title: How the eye forms images
basics: The cornea and lens focus light onto the retina, where photoreceptors convert it into nerve signals. The brain assembles these into what we see.
deeper: Rhodopsin changes shape when it absorbs a photon, triggering a chemical cascade. Three cone types give colour vision.
expert: Eye focal length ≈17 mm (≈60 D); cone peaks ≈420, 534, 564 nm; retinal isomerisation 11-cis→all-trans.
regime: Optical limits set by pupil diffraction and cone spacing (~2 μm).

title: Sound and hearing
basics: Sound is pressure waves in air; the ear converts them into nerve signals. Pitch depends on frequency and loudness on amplitude.
deeper: Different places on the cochlear membrane resonate at different frequencies. Loudness is measured in decibels.
expert: dB=10 log(I/I₀), I₀=10⁻¹² W/m²; threshold ≈20 μPa; speech 0.3–3 kHz; cochlea length ≈35 mm.
regime: Hearing declines with age and noise exposure.

title: Memory and learning
basics: Memory has working memory (a few items), and long-term memory consolidated during sleep. Learning links stimuli and rewards.
deeper: Dopamine signals reward-prediction errors that drive reinforcement learning. Spaced practice improves retention.
expert: Working memory ≈4 chunks; Ebbinghaus forgetting curve R=e^{−t/S}; Rescorla-Wagner ΔV=αβ(λ−ΣV).
regime: Models describe typical behaviour; individual variation is large.

frontier.text: How memories are physically stored and how consolidation during sleep works
Whether engram-based storage generalises across memory types

title: Cognition, emotion and behaviour
basics: Psychology studies perception, thinking, emotion and personality. Reliable findings include limited attention, heuristics and biases, and conditioning.
deeper: Twin studies find that for many traits about 30–60 % of the variation between people in a given population is statistically linked to genetic differences; this says nothing about how much of one person's trait is genetic.
expert: Twin studies h² for IQ ≈0.5–0.8 in adults; Kahneman-Tversky prospect theory; Big Five traits.
regime: Findings must be judged one by one; many classic effects failed replication.

title: The replication crisis
basics: Large replication projects found that many published psychology results shrink or disappear when repeated. Ego depletion and power posing are examples.
deeper: Small samples, flexible analysis and publication bias inflate false positives. Pre-registration and larger studies are the main remedies.
expert: Open Science Collaboration 2015: ≈36 % of 100 replications significant vs 97 % original; effect size halved.
regime: Rates differ between fields and methods.

title: Consciousness
basics: Why brain activity comes with subjective experience is unsolved. Rival theories include integrated information, global neuronal workspace, higher-order and predictive-processing views.
deeper: Experiments compare brain activity for stimuli that are seen versus unseen. No consensus theory exists, and no test settles whether a machine could be conscious.
expert: Integrated information Φ (IIT); global workspace theory predicts a late "ignition" (≈300–500 ms after the stimulus, often linked to the P3b), but whether the P3b marks conscious access or later report-related processing is itself disputed.
regime: Measurement problem: reports versus experience.

title: Predictive processing in the brain
basics: One influential idea says the brain constantly predicts its inputs and learns from errors. It links perception, action and learning in one framework.
deeper: The free-energy principle formalises this. Evidence is mixed and the idea is hard to falsify.
expert: Free energy F=E_q[ln q(s)−ln p(o,s)]; prediction error ε=o−ĝ(μ).
regime: Framework status, not confirmed mechanism.

title: Sleep and circadian rhythms
basics: Sleep follows a roughly 24-hour clock driven by cells in the brain and genes that cycle in expression. Sleep supports memory consolidation and many other processes; a role in clearing metabolic waste from the brain has been proposed, but the evidence is disputed.
deeper: Light resets the clock via special retinal cells. Lack of sleep impairs attention and health.
expert: Circadian period ≈24.2 h; REM cycles ≈90 min; adults need ≈7–9 h; melatonin peaks at night.
regime: Exact functions of sleep are not fully known.

title: Ecosystems and energy flow
basics: Ecosystems get energy from sunlight, and only about 10 % passes from each feeding level to the next. This limits how many top predators can exist.
deeper: Producers capture light, consumers eat them, and decomposers recycle nutrients. Food webs link species in complex networks.
expert: Transfer efficiency ≈10 % (range 5–20 %); global NPP ≈105 Pg C/yr (land ≈55, ocean ≈50); only ≈0.1 % of incident sunlight ends up as global net primary production (≈1 % in the best crop stands).
regime: Efficiency varies with ecosystem.

title: Population dynamics and species interactions
basics: Populations grow until limited by food or space. Predators and prey, competitors and partners shape each other's numbers.
deeper: The logistic equation and Lotka-Volterra models capture basic cycles. Mutualism, parasitism and competition appear throughout nature.
expert: dN/dt=rN(1−N/K); Lotka-Volterra ẋ=αx−βxy, ẏ=δxy−γy; r–K selection (a historical scheme, now mostly superseded by age-structured life-history theory).
regime: Real populations show noise, age structure, and chaos in some cases.

title: Biodiversity, extinction and conservation
basics: Species richness rises with area and falls with isolation (island biogeography). Current extinction rates are far above the long-term background.
deeper: Habitat loss, overharvest, invasive species, pollution and climate change are the main pressures. Ecosystems provide services such as pollination and water filtering.
expert: Species-area S=cA^z, z≈0.25; background extinction ≈0.1–1 per million species-years.
regime: Rates for poorly known groups are uncertain.

frontier.text: Predicting ecosystem response to warming and extinctions

title: Life reshaping Earth: oxygenation
basics: Cyanobacteria released oxygen, and the air changed chemically about 2.4 billion years ago in the Great Oxidation Event. Oxygen was needed for complex life but was not sufficient for it to arise immediately.
deeper: Banded iron formations record the oxygen sink. Later, plants on land changed erosion and the carbon cycle.
expert: O₂ rose from <10⁻⁵ to ≈1–10 % of present level around 2.4–2.1 Ga; present 21 %.
regime: Timing and rate of oxygenation debated in detail.

frontier.text: When did oxygenic photosynthesis arise (before the Great Oxidation Event, with "whiffs" of oxygen in the Archean)?
Why did oxygen stay near 1–10 % of the present level until about 0.6 billion years ago?

title: Minerals and the rock cycle
basics: Rocks are aggregates of minerals, which are crystalline solids with defined chemistry. The three rock families (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic) transform into one another over geological time.
deeper: Silicates make up most of the crust; quartz, feldspar and olivine are common. Melting, burial, uplift and erosion cycle the material.
expert: Crust ≈47 % O, 28 % Si, 8 % Al, 5 % Fe by mass; quartz SiO₂ Mohs 7; olivine (Mg,Fe)₂SiO₄; granite ρ≈2.7, basalt ρ≈3.0 g/cm³.
regime: Classification is by origin, not composition alone.

title: Earth's interior
basics: Earth has a thin crust, a thick convecting rocky mantle, a liquid outer core and a solid inner core. Seismic waves reveal this layering.
deeper: Core is mainly iron and nickel. The inner core is solid because of pressure despite temperatures near the Sun's surface.
expert: R=6371 km; crust 5–70 km; mantle to 2891 km; outer core to 5150 km; inner core r≈1220 km; core T≈5000–6000 K; P_center≈364 GPa.
regime: Composition details (light elements in core) uncertain; inner-core dynamics debated.

title: Plate tectonics
basics: Earth's rigid outer shell is broken into about 15 plates that drift a few centimetres a year. Plate motions build mountains, open oceans and cause earthquakes and volcanoes.
deeper: Plates form at spreading ridges, slide past at transform faults and sink at subduction zones. Mantle convection and slab pull drive them.
expert: Speeds 1–10 cm/yr (Atlantic ≈2.5, Pacific ≈7–10); oceanic crust ≤≈180 Myr; Wilson cycle ≈300–500 Myr.
regime: When plate tectonics started (between ~4 and 2.5 Ga) is debated.

title: Earthquakes and seismic waves
basics: Earthquakes release energy stored by slowly moving rock when a fault suddenly slips. Seismic waves of several types spread out and are recorded worldwide.
deeper: P waves compress, S waves shear (not through liquid) and surface waves cause most damage. Magnitude is logarithmic: each unit means ≈32 times more energy.
expert: log E=1.5M+4.8 (J); M₀=μAD; v_P≈6–8 km/s crust; v_S≈3.5–4.5 km/s; Gutenberg-Richter log N=a−bM, b≈1.
regime: Earthquakes can be forecast only probabilistically.

title: Volcanoes and magma
basics: Volcanoes erupt where molten rock rises to the surface at plate boundaries and hot spots. Gas content and viscosity decide whether an eruption is gentle or explosive.
deeper: Basaltic magma flows easily and forms shields; silica-rich magma is sticky and traps gas, giving explosive eruptions. Eruptions release aerosols that can cool climate temporarily.
expert: Basalt lava ≈1100–1250 °C; Pinatubo 1991 cooled global mean ≈0.5 °C for ≈2 yr; VEI scale logarithmic.
regime: Timing of eruptions is hard to predict.

title: Mountain building
basics: Colliding plates push up mountains, while rain, ice, rivers and wind wear them down and carry sediment to the sea. Chemical weathering also removes CO₂ from air.
deeper: Collision thickens the crust; isostasy keeps thick crust high, and erosion removes material at a rate set by relief and climate. Uplift and erosion balance over millions of years. Weathering of silicate rocks is a slow thermostat for climate.
expert: Himalaya uplift ≈5 mm/yr; erosion rates 0.01–1 mm/yr; CaSiO₃+CO₂→CaCO₃+SiO₂.
regime: Rates vary with climate and lithology.

title: Sedimentary processes and soils
basics: Broken-down rock is carried by water and wind, deposited in layers, and cemented into sedimentary rock. Soil forms where rock, air, water and life interact.
deeper: Soil layers (horizons) hold nutrients and water that plants rely on. A centimetre of soil can take hundreds of years to form.
expert: Soil formation ≈0.01–0.1 mm/yr; USDA texture classes: clay <2 μm, silt 2–50 μm, sand 50 μm–2 mm; soil organic C ≈1,500 Pg in the top 1 m (about 2,400 Pg to 2 m).
regime: Rates vary widely with climate.

title: Soil as a living system
basics: A handful of soil holds billions of microbes, fungi and tiny animals that recycle nutrients and feed plants. Fungal networks physically connect many plant roots; whether they carry significant nutrients or signals between plants in nature is debated.
deeper: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules supply plants with ammonia. Soil carbon is a major store.
expert: ≈10⁸–10⁹ bacteria per gram; fungal hyphae ≈10–1000 m per gram of soil depending on soil type; soil pH 4–9.
regime: Complex, hard to model at ecosystem scale.

frontier.text: Do mycorrhizal networks transfer significant nutrients or signals between plants in natural ecosystems?

title: Deep time and Earth's history
basics: Earth is about 4.54 billion years old. Layers of rock and fossils record eras from the Hadean through the Phanerozoic.
deeper: Index fossils and radiometric dates build the geologic time scale. Major events include the Moon-forming impact, first life, oxygenation and mass extinctions.
expert: Earth 4.54 Gyr; oldest rocks ≈4.0 Gyr; oldest zircons 4.4 Gyr; Cambrian start 538.8 Ma; Chicxulub 66.0 Ma.
regime: Early-Earth record is sparse.

title: Earth's magnetic field and the geodynamo
basics: Moving liquid iron in the outer core generates Earth's magnetic field, which shields the surface from charged particles. The field flips polarity at irregular intervals.
deeper: Convection driven by heat and crystallisation of the inner core, together with rotation, sustains the dynamo. Auroras are caused by solar particles funnelled along field lines.
expert: Surface field ≈25–65 μT; dipole moment ≈8×10²² A m²; reversals average about every 0.25 Myr over the last 10 Myr, but are irregular, with superchrons lasting tens of Myr; the last was Matuyama–Brunhes at ≈773 ka.
regime: Numerical dynamos reproduce key features; detailed mechanisms of reversals are debated.

title: Ocean circulation
basics: Ocean water moves in surface gyres driven by wind and in deep currents driven by differences in temperature and saltiness. This circulation carries heat from the tropics to higher latitudes.
deeper: Coriolis deflection and continents shape currents like the Gulf Stream. Deep water forms in the North Atlantic and around Antarctica and returns over several centuries to about a thousand years.
expert: Gulf Stream ≈30 Sv (1 Sv=10⁶ m³/s); AMOC ≈17 Sv; ocean covers 71 % of Earth, mean depth ≈3.7 km; thermohaline turnover ≈1000 yr.
regime: Models resolve large-scale flows; eddy parametrisation is an uncertainty.

title: Tides
basics: The Moon's gravity pulls more on the near side of Earth than the far side, stretching the oceans into two bulges. Most coasts see two high tides a day.
deeper: The Sun adds a smaller pull, giving spring and neap tides. Tidal friction slowly lengthens Earth's day and pushes the Moon away.
expert: Tidal acceleration ∝GMr/d³; Moon recedes ≈3.8 cm/yr; lunar tide ≈2.2× solar; ocean range 0.5–16 m.
regime: Local tides depend on coast shape and resonance.

title: Coriolis effect
basics: On a rotating Earth, moving air and water curve to the right in the northern hemisphere and to the left in the southern. This makes cyclones spin.
deeper: It is an apparent force from viewing motion in a rotating frame. It is negligible in a sink but dominates large weather systems.
expert: a=−2Ω×v; f=2Ω sinφ, Ω=7.292×10⁻⁵ rad/s; f vanishes at the equator, so tropical cyclones do not form within about 5° of it; Rossby number Ro=U/fL.
regime: Only matters for large scales or long times.

title: Structure of the atmosphere
basics: Earth's atmosphere has layers: troposphere (weather), stratosphere (ozone layer), mesosphere and thermosphere. Half the air lies below about 5.5 km.
deeper: Temperature falls with height in the troposphere by about 6.5 °C per km, rises in the stratosphere because ozone absorbs UV, and again in the thermosphere.
expert: Troposphere top ≈8–9 km at the poles to ≈16–18 km in the tropics (mean ≈11–12 km); P(z)=P₀e^{−z/H}, H≈8.4 km; lapse rate Γ≈6.5 K/km (dry adiabatic 9.8 K/km); Kármán line 100 km.
regime: Boundaries vary with latitude and season.

title: The greenhouse effect
basics: Gases like water vapour, carbon dioxide and methane let sunlight in but absorb heat leaving the surface, keeping Earth about 33 °C warmer than the 255 K it would have at its present albedo if the atmosphere absorbed no infrared.
deeper: Adding more CO₂ reduces outgoing radiation until the planet warms to rebalance. The effect was first described by Fourier, Tyndall and Arrhenius.
expert: T_eff=[S(1−α)/4σ]^{1/4}=255 K, with S=1361 W/m² the solar constant and α≈0.30 the albedo; surface 288 K; ΔF≈5.35 ln(C/C₀) W/m² for CO₂; ≈3.7 W/m² per doubling.
regime: Radiative physics is solid; feedbacks (clouds, ice) set the response.

title: Weather systems and global circulation
basics: Heating differences between the equator and poles drive large cells of circulation (Hadley, Ferrel, polar) and jet streams. Fronts and storms form where air masses meet.
deeper: Rotation bends flow into winds and storms. Water vapour condensation releases heat that fuels thunderstorms and hurricanes.
expert: Hadley cell extends ≈0–30° lat; jet core ≈10–15 km altitude, speeds ≈50–100 m/s; hurricane wind ≥33 m/s.
regime: Chaotic: small errors grow, limiting detailed forecasts to roughly 2 weeks.

title: Weather and clouds
basics: Weather arises when air rises, cools and its water vapour condenses into clouds and precipitation. Warm, moist air carries the energy.
deeper: Cloud droplets (≈10 μm) need condensation nuclei like dust and sea salt. In warm clouds droplets grow by collision and coalescence. In cold clouds ice crystals grow at the droplets' expense and melt as they fall. Raindrops are typically 0.5–5 mm.
expert: Latent heat L_v=2.5 MJ/kg; Clausius-Clapeyron: saturation vapour pressure rises ≈7 %/K; cloud droplet ≈10 μm, raindrop ≈1 mm.
regime: Microphysics parameterised in models.

title: Weather forecasting
basics: Forecasts run physical equations on computers starting from observations. Useful skill for large systems is about 7–10 days, and the theoretical predictability limit (Lorenz) is about 2 weeks.
deeper: Machine-learning models trained on past weather now rival physics-based ones for some measures. Ensembles show uncertainty.
expert: Lorenz limit ≈2 weeks; forecast skill has gained about one day of lead time per decade since the 1980s (Bauer et al. 2015); grid ≈9 km (ECMWF HRES).
regime: Extreme events and local convection remain hard.
evidence: Bauer, Thorpe and Brunet 2015, Nature (the quiet revolution of numerical weather prediction)

title: Tropical cyclones and severe storms
basics: Hurricanes draw energy from warm ocean water (above ~26.5 °C) and spin because of Earth's rotation. Thunderstorms form when warm moist air rises rapidly.
deeper: Wind strength, rain and storm surge cause damage. Warmer seas favour more intense storms, though trends in frequency are uncertain.
expert: Wind ≥119 km/h for hurricane; latent-heat release ≈6×10¹⁴ W (≈5×10¹⁹ J/day), of which wind kinetic energy is ≈10¹² W (about 0.25 %); storm surge several metres for major landfalls, with records above 8 m (Katrina 2005 ≈8.5 m); SST threshold ≈26.5 °C.
regime: Link to climate change is robust for intensity, less certain for frequency.

title: The water cycle
basics: Water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as rain or snow, and flows back to the sea. Sunlight drives the cycle, and nearly all of Earth's water is in the oceans.
deeper: Residence times range from days in the atmosphere to thousands of years in deep ice and groundwater.
expert: Oceans 97 %, ice ≈2 %, fresh liquid <1 %; evaporation ≈5×10⁵ km³/yr; atmosphere holds ≈1.3×10⁴ km³ (≈9-day residence).
regime: Human withdrawals alter flows locally.

title: Carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus cycles
basics: Elements circulate between rock, ocean, air and living things. These cycles connect geology to biology and set climate over long times.
deeper: Carbon moves between air, oceans, plants and rocks; nitrogen is fixed by microbes and human industry; phosphorus comes mainly from rock weathering and limits growth in many places.
expert: Atmospheric C ≈ 850 Pg; ocean ≈38 000 Pg; land plants ≈450–650 Pg; fossil-fuel emissions ≈ 10 Pg C/yr in recent decades; N fixation by industry ≈ natural land fixation.
regime: Atmospheric stocks and fossil emissions are known to a few %, but many natural fluxes (biological N fixation, the land sink, phosphorus) are uncertain by 30 % to a factor of 2.

title: The nitrogen cycle
basics: Nitrogen gas is turned into usable ammonia by bacteria and lightning, then cycles through plants and animals and is returned to air by denitrifying microbes.
deeper: Fertiliser runoff causes eutrophication. Humans have roughly doubled the amount of reactive nitrogen entering ecosystems.
expert: N fixation: terrestrial natural ≈58 (range 40–100) Tg N/yr plus lightning ≈5; industrial (Haber–Bosch) ≈120 Tg N/yr in 2010, ≈150 Tg N/yr in recent years; nitrogenase requires 16 ATP per N₂.
regime: Budgets uncertain.

title: The carbon cycle and CO₂ in the atmosphere
basics: Carbon dioxide is exchanged between air, oceans and plants. Burning fossil fuels and clearing forests has raised atmospheric CO₂ far above the pre-industrial level of about 280 ppm.
deeper: About half of emitted CO₂ stays in the air; the rest is absorbed by ocean and land. The seasonal sawtooth in the Mauna Loa record reflects Northern Hemisphere plant growth.
expert: Pre-industrial ≈280 ppm; Mauna Loa passed 400 ppm in 2013; ≈2.1 Pg C per ppm; airborne fraction ≈0.45; isotope δ¹³C shows fossil origin.
regime: Future sinks depend on warming, ocean chemistry and land use.

title: Ocean acidification
basics: Seawater absorbs CO₂, which forms carbonic acid and lowers pH. Since the pre-industrial era surface pH has fallen by about 0.1 units, roughly a 30 % rise in acidity.
deeper: More acidity makes it harder for corals, shellfish and some plankton to build calcium-carbonate shells.
expert: CO₂+H₂O⇌H₂CO₃⇌H⁺+HCO₃⁻; pH 8.2→8.1; [H⁺] +≈30 %; saturation state Ω=[Ca²⁺][CO₃²⁻]/K_sp.
regime: Buffering varies regionally.

title: The climate system and global warming
basics: Earth's climate is set by sunlight, atmosphere, oceans, ice and life. Human activity has unequivocally warmed the planet: about 1.1 °C by 2011–2020 (IPCC AR6) and about 1.2 °C over 2015–2024 relative to 1850–1900, with 2024 the first calendar year about 1.5 °C above that baseline.
deeper: Energy imbalance mostly goes into the oceans (about 90 %). Feedbacks like melting ice and water vapour amplify warming, while aerosols cool by about −1.3 W/m² (−2.0 to −0.6), masking part of the greenhouse forcing. Equilibrium climate sensitivity is likely 2.5–4 °C per CO₂ doubling, best estimate 3 °C (IPCC AR6).
expert: Radiative forcing F; ΔT=λF with equilibrium sensitivity λ; Earth energy imbalance ≈0.5–1 W/m²; global mean sea-level rise ≈3.3 mm/yr over 1993–2018 and ≈4–5 mm/yr in the most recent decade.
regime: Physics solid; regional details and tipping thresholds uncertain.

frontier.text: Tipping elements (ice sheets, Amazon, permafrost, reefs)

title: Ice ages and orbital cycles
basics: Slow changes in Earth's orbit and tilt alter how sunlight is spread over latitude and season, pacing the ice ages. Feedbacks from CO₂ and ice amplify these small changes.
deeper: Cycles of about 100, 41 and 21 thousand years appear in ocean sediments and ice cores.
expert: Eccentricity ≈100 & 400 kyr; obliquity 22.1–24.5°, 41 kyr; precession ≈19–23 kyr; glacial CO₂ ≈180 vs interglacial ≈280 ppm.
regime: Why the 100-kyr cycle dominates in the last million years is still debated.

title: Ice sheets and sea level
basics: Ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica hold enough water to raise sea level by about 65 metres if fully melted. Glaciers flow slowly under their own weight.
deeper: Warming ocean water can undercut floating ice shelves, speeding up flow. Sea level also rises because water expands when it warms.
expert: Greenland ≈7.4 m, West Antarctic ≈5 m, East Antarctic ≈53 m SLE; Glen's flow law: strain rate ε̇=Aτⁿ with n≈3 (A depends strongly on temperature).
regime: Rate of future ice loss is the largest uncertainty in sea-level projections.

title: Atlantic overturning circulation (AMOC)
basics: The Atlantic overturning circulation brings warm water north and sends cold deep water south. It contributes to the mild climate of northwestern Europe, though most of that mildness comes from atmospheric transport and the ocean's heat storage.
deeper: Freshwater from melting ice could weaken it. How close it is to a tipping point is debated.
expert: ≈17 Sv at 26.5°N; heat transport ≈1.2 PW; Stommel bistable model.
regime: Short observational record limits conclusions.

frontier.text: Timing and reversibility of any collapse

title: The ozone layer
basics: A thin layer of ozone in the stratosphere absorbs most harmful ultraviolet light. Industrial chlorofluorocarbons broke it down, creating the Antarctic ozone hole.
deeper: The Montreal Protocol phased out these chemicals and the layer is slowly recovering.
expert: O₃ peak ≈ 20–25 km; column ≈300 DU (Dobson units); O₃+hν(<310 nm); Cl catalytic cycle: Cl+O₃→ClO+O₂.
regime: Per WMO/UNEP 2022: recovery to 1980 levels around 2040 (global), 2045 (Arctic) and 2066 (Antarctic).

title: Formation of the Solar System
basics: The Sun and planets formed about 4.57 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust. Dust stuck together into planetesimals, then planets.
deeper: Rocky planets formed near the Sun where it was too hot for ice; giants formed beyond the snow line. Giant planets may have migrated, as in the Nice model.
expert: Age 4.568 Gyr (CAIs); snow line ≈2.7–5 AU depending on the disc model (about 2.7 AU in the classic minimum-mass nebula); disk mass ≈0.01–0.1 M☉; pebble accretion; Hill radius r_H=a(m/3M)^{1/3}.
regime: Broad picture solid; migration histories debated.

title: Planets: rocky, giant and ice
basics: Terrestrial planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are small and rocky; Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants; Uranus and Neptune are ice giants. Each differs in atmosphere, interior and history.
deeper: Mass and distance from the Sun decide what a planet can hold. Venus's runaway greenhouse shows how atmosphere can transform a world.
expert: Radii (km): Mercury 2440, Venus 6052, Earth 6371, Mars 3390, Jupiter 69911, Saturn 58232, Uranus 25362, Neptune 24622; Venus surface ≈737 K, 92 bar.
regime: Properties well measured by spacecraft.

title: Origin of the Moon
basics: The Moon likely formed when a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth. Lunar rocks are surprisingly similar in isotopes to Earth's, which challenges simple versions of this model.
deeper: Alternatives and refinements include a vaporised donut-shaped structure, a faster-spinning Earth, or multiple impacts.
expert: M_Moon=0.0123 M_E; mean distance 384 400 km; Earth-Moon angular momentum 3.5×10³⁴ kg m²/s; Apollo samples ≈4.35–4.5 Gyr.
regime: Giant impact is consensus in outline; details debated.

frontier.text: Which kind of impact formed the Moon (a fast-spinning Earth, a synestia or multiple smaller impacts) and how its isotopes came to match Earth's so closely

title: Where did Earth's water come from?
basics: Water may have arrived with asteroids rich in water, been built into Earth's rocky ingredients, or both. Comets contribute little by their isotopic ratios.
deeper: Hydrogen isotope ratios (D/H) match carbonaceous chondrites but not 67P-type comets. Enstatite chondrites, which formed near Earth's own orbit, also hold enough hydrogen to supply several oceans (Piani et al., Science 2020), so some water may be native.
expert: Ocean D/H≈1.56×10⁻⁴ (VSMOW); carbonaceous chondrites ≈1.4–1.7×10⁻⁴; comet 67P ≈5.3×10⁻⁴.
regime: Mixed sources likely.

title: Moons, tidal heating and rings
basics: Moons orbiting giant planets are squeezed and flexed by tides. This heats Io into the most volcanic body known and keeps oceans liquid under the ice of Europa and Enceladus.
deeper: Tidal flexing heats a moon only if its orbit stays eccentric. For Io, Europa and Ganymede the Laplace resonance keeps it so, which is why Io's surface heat flow reaches ≈2 W/m². Giant planets also have rings made of ice and rock particles, and Titan has a thick atmosphere and methane lakes.
expert: Io heat flow ≈2 W/m²; Enceladus plume ≈200 kg/s; Saturn main rings ≈7×10⁴–1.4×10⁵ km from centre, typical thickness ≈10–20 m.
regime: Presence of oceans inferred from gravity/magnetism and plumes.

title: Asteroids, comets and impacts
basics: Asteroids and comets are leftover building blocks. Asteroids are rocky or metallic, comets icy; both leave craters when they hit planets.
deeper: Most asteroids lie between Mars and Jupiter. The Kuiper belt and Oort cloud hold icy bodies. Impacts shaped planetary surfaces; the one 66 Myr ago ended the age of non-avian dinosaurs.
expert: Main belt 2.1–3.3 AU; Ceres 940 km; KE=½mv² (10 km body at 20 km/s ≈10²³ J); Kuiper belt 30–50 AU; Oort cloud ≈2000–10⁵ AU.
regime: Impact rates well constrained for recent times.

title: Exoplanets
basics: Thousands of planets have been found around other stars using tiny dips in starlight (transits) and star wobbles (radial velocity). Planet types not in our system, like super-Earths, are the most common.
deeper: Statistics show most stars host planets. JWST is beginning to read atmospheres of some of them.
expert: Transit depth ≈(R_p/R_*)²; RV semi-amplitude K=28.4 m/s ×(M_p sin i/M_J)(P/1yr)^{-1/3}(M_*/M☉)^{-2/3}(1−e²)^{-1/2}, for M_p≪M_*.
regime: Detection biases favour large, close-in planets.

title: Habitable zones and astrobiology
basics: The habitable zone is the range of distances where a planet could have liquid surface water. Life elsewhere is possible but not detected.
deeper: Claims of biosignatures, such as gases in atmospheres, need careful testing against non-biological explanations.
expert: HZ inner edge ≈0.95 AU, outer ≈1.4–1.7 AU for Sun-like star; Drake equation N=R*·fp·ne·fl·fi·fc·L.
regime: The habitable zone only means a rocky planet with an Earth-like atmosphere could hold surface liquid water. It is neither necessary nor sufficient for life. No extraterrestrial life is confirmed.

frontier.text: Biosignature claims (e.g. phosphine on Venus, DMS on K2-18b) remain unconfirmed

title: The Sun
basics: The Sun is a middle-aged star that shines by fusing hydrogen in its core. Energy made in the core takes tens of thousands of years or more (one standard estimate: about 170,000 years) to reach the surface by radiation and convection.
deeper: Its surface (photosphere) is about 5800 K, with sunspots, flares and a million-degree corona. The solar wind fills the heliosphere.
expert: L☉=3.828×10²⁶ W; R☉=6.957×10⁸ m; M☉=1.989×10³⁰ kg; T_c≈1.57×10⁷ K; ρ_c≈150 g/cm³; photon diffusion time ≈10⁴–1.7×10⁵ yr depending on the model; 11-yr cycle.
regime: Coronal heating mechanism still debated.

title: Stellar structure and hydrostatic equilibrium
basics: A star is a balance between gravity pulling inward and pressure pushing outward. Fusion in the core keeps the pressure up.
deeper: More massive stars burn hotter and much brighter, so they live shorter lives. This is the mass-luminosity relation.
expert: dP/dr=−Gmρ/r²; L∝M^{3.5} (main sequence); lifetime t≈10 Gyr(M/M☉)^{−2.5} for roughly 0.5–10 M☉, while for M≳25 M☉ lifetimes level off at about 3–7 Myr; virial 2K+U=0.
regime: Simplified for spherical, non-rotating stars.

title: Stellar spectra and the H-R diagram
basics: Starlight spectra reveal temperature, composition and motion. Plotting luminosity against temperature groups stars into a main sequence, giants and white dwarfs.
deeper: Spectral types O B A F G K M run from hot to cool. Doppler shifts tell speed and binary orbits.
expert: L=4πR²σT⁴; M_V=m−5log(d/10 pc); B−V color index; spectral types O ≳30 000 K to M ≲3 500 K.
regime: Metallicity and rotation modify lines.

title: Star formation and the interstellar medium
basics: Stars form when cold dense clouds of gas and dust collapse under their own gravity. The space between stars contains gas, dust and cosmic rays.
deeper: Collapse needs the cloud to be massive enough (Jeans mass). Protostars grow with disks and jets.
expert: Jeans mass M_J≈(5kT/Gμm_H)^{3/2}(3/4πρ)^{1/2}; molecular cloud T≈10 K, n≈10²–10⁶ cm⁻³; star formation efficiency ≈1–10 %.
regime: Role of magnetic fields and turbulence still studied.
evidence: Infrared and radio observations of Orion

title: Stellar evolution
basics: After hydrogen runs out in the core, stars expand into giants. Sun-like stars end as white dwarfs; massive stars explode as supernovae.
deeper: Nuclear burning proceeds through helium, carbon and heavier fuel in massive stars, ending with an iron core.
expert: Sun leaves main sequence in ≈5 Gyr; M<8 M☉→white dwarf (<1.4 M☉ Chandrasekhar); M>8 M☉→core-collapse; 25 M☉ lifetime ≈ 7 Myr.
regime: Mass loss, rotation and binarity change tracks.

title: White dwarfs, supernovae and neutron stars
basics: Dead stars become dense remnants: white dwarfs supported by electron degeneracy, or neutron stars and black holes after core-collapse supernovae.
deeper: A teaspoon of neutron-star matter weighs about a billion tonnes. Pulsars are spinning neutron stars with beams.
expert: WD: M≈0.6 M☉, R≈R⊕, M_Ch=1.4 M☉; NS: M≈1.4–2 M☉, R≈11–13 km, mean density ≈4×10¹⁷ kg/m³ (up to ≈10¹⁸ kg/m³ at the centre), so a teaspoon is about 10⁹–10¹⁰ tonnes; core-collapse supernova releases ≈10⁴⁶ J (≈99 % as neutrinos), of which ≈10⁴⁴ J (1 foe) is ejecta kinetic energy and ≈10⁴²–10⁴³ J is light.
regime: Neutron-star equation of state uncertain.

title: Origin of the chemical elements
basics: The Big Bang made hydrogen, helium and a little lithium; stars forged carbon through iron; most heavier elements are built by capturing neutrons, either slowly (the s-process, in giant stars late in their lives) or rapidly (the r-process, in neutron-rich events such as neutron-star mergers and possibly some supernovae).
deeper: We are made of star-processed material. How much of the heaviest elements comes from mergers versus other supernovae is still debated.
expert: Solar photosphere by mass (Asplund et al. 2009): H 73.8 %, He 24.9 %, O 0.57 %, C 0.24 %; BBN D/H≈2.5×10⁻⁵, ⁷Li shortfall ≈3×; r-process peaks A≈80, 130, 195. The s-process in low- and intermediate-mass asymptotic-giant-branch stars and the r-process together produce the bulk of the heavy elements in the solar system (review: Kobayashi, Karakas and Lugaro 2020, ApJ 900, 179).
regime: Sources of r-process elements debated.

frontier.text: Neutron-star mergers vs collapsars for r-process

title: Kilonovae and heavy elements
basics: When two neutron stars merge, they emit gravitational waves, a burst of gamma rays and a glow powered by freshly made heavy elements such as gold.
deeper: GW170817 was seen in both gravitational waves and light, confirming such events create r-process elements.
expert: GW170817: 1.17–1.60 M☉ components, d≈40 Mpc, ejecta ≈0.05 M☉; AT2017gfo (the kilonova) peak bolometric luminosity ≈ a few 10⁴¹ to 10⁴² erg/s (≈10³⁵ W) within about 1 day, depending on the reconstruction.
regime: Event rate and yields uncertain.

title: Binary and variable stars
basics: About half of Sun-like stars (≈44 ± 2 %) have at least one stellar companion. Variable stars such as Cepheids pulse in a way that reveals their true brightness, used as cosmic distance markers.
deeper: Binaries let astronomers weigh stars directly. Type Ia supernovae from white dwarfs in binaries act as standard candles.
expert: Cepheid P-L: M_V≈−2.43(log P−1)−4.05; SN Ia peak M_B≈−19.3 (after light-curve standardisation; raw spread about 0.4 mag).
regime: Calibration of standard candles underlies the Hubble tension.

title: The cosmic distance ladder
basics: Astronomers measure distances stepwise: parallax for nearby stars, standard candles like Cepheids for galaxies, then supernovae and redshift for the far universe.
deeper: Each rung calibrates the next, so errors propagate upward. Gaia has measured parallaxes for over a billion stars.
expert: d(pc)=1/p(arcsec); m−M=5log₁₀(d/10pc); for a flat universe d_L=(1+z)∫₀^z c dz′/H(z′).
regime: Systematics at each rung are debated.

title: The Milky Way galaxy
basics: Our galaxy is a barred spiral of a few hundred billion stars about 100,000 light-years across, with the Sun about 27,000 light-years from the centre. The Sun orbits the centre once in about 230 million years; stars closer in orbit faster.
deeper: Stars orbit the centre once every ~230 million years. A supermassive black hole, Sgr A*, sits at the centre.
expert: Disk diameter ≈30 kpc; R☉≈8.2 kpc; v_circ≈230 km/s; M_stars≈6×10¹⁰ M☉; Sgr A* ≈4.3×10⁶ M☉; halo mass ≈10¹² M☉.
regime: Mass of halo depends on dark matter modelling.

title: Galaxies and the cosmic web
basics: Galaxies are huge collections of stars, gas and dark matter. They come as spirals, ellipticals and irregulars, and are organised into groups, clusters and filaments.
deeper: Galaxies form inside dark-matter halos and grow by mergers. Open puzzles include cusp-core and satellite counts, and early galaxies that look surprisingly mature.
expert: Typical L*≈2×10¹⁰ L☉; cluster mass ≈10¹⁴–10¹⁵ M☉; Local Group diameter ≈3 Mpc; filaments tens of Mpc.
regime: Hierarchical picture well supported; small-scale tensions remain.

frontier.text: Cusp-core, too-big-to-fail and satellite-plane problems (the original "missing satellites" count has largely been resolved by faint-dwarf discoveries and baryonic feedback)

title: Dark matter
basics: Galaxies rotate too fast and clusters bend light too strongly for the visible matter alone, so about 85 % of matter appears to be non-luminous 'dark matter'. What it is remains unknown.
deeper: Candidates include WIMPs, axions, sterile neutrinos and primordial black holes. Modified gravity (MOND) fits galaxies but has trouble with clusters and the CMB.
expert: Flat rotation curves v≈const; Ω_cdm h²=0.120; Ω_b h²=0.0224; Bullet Cluster lens-mass offset.
regime: Existence well supported; identity unknown.

title: Active galaxies and quasars
basics: Some galaxies have extremely bright centres powered by gas falling into a supermassive black hole. Quasars outshine whole galaxies.
deeper: Jets of plasma travel near light speed. Black-hole mass correlates with the host galaxy's bulge.
expert: L_Edd=4πGMm_pc/σ_T=1.26×10³¹ W (M/M☉), for spherical accretion of ionised hydrogen (discs can exceed it briefly); efficiency η≈0.06–0.4; M-σ relation.
regime: Accretion physics is complex.

title: Supermassive black hole growth and early galaxies
basics: Giant black holes already existed less than a billion years after the Big Bang, which challenges simple growth models. JWST has found compact red sources that may be linked.
deeper: Possible routes are heavy seeds from direct collapse, rapid accretion, or mergers of lighter seeds.
expert: Sgr A* ≈4.3×10⁶ M☉; quasars at z>7 with M≈10⁹ M☉ within 0.7 Gyr; Salpeter time t_S=450 Myr·η/(1−η).
regime: Open question; measurements of black-hole masses in early objects are uncertain.

frontier.text: How early black holes grew so fast

title: Expansion of the universe
basics: Distant galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther they are the faster they go. This is explained by space itself expanding.
deeper: Light stretches as space expands, shifting it to longer wavelengths (redshift). The expansion rate today is the Hubble constant.
expert: v≈cz=H₀d for z≪1 (d≪c/H₀≈4 Gpc); at larger distances use the full expansion history d_L=(1+z)∫c dz/H(z); 1+z=a₀/a; H₀≈67–74 km/s/Mpc (two methods disagree); Hubble time 1/H₀≈14 Gyr.
regime: Expansion applies on scales beyond bound systems.

title: The Hubble tension
basics: Two ways of measuring how fast the universe expands, one from the early universe and one from nearby objects, give different answers. Whether this is new physics or measurement error is unresolved.
deeper: Proposed fixes include early dark energy or extra relativistic particles, none confirmed.
expert: Planck 2018 ΛCDM: H₀=67.4±0.5 km/s/Mpc; SH0ES Cepheid-SN ladder ≈73 km/s/Mpc (≈5σ gap).
regime: The tension depends on the calibration route: Cepheid and supernova ladders give ≈73 km/s/Mpc, CMB-based ΛCDM gives ≈67.4, and TRGB/JWST analyses (CCHP) give values in between. The apparent tension is about 5σ for the Cepheid ladder and smaller for TRGB. The open-questions list has newer measurements.

title: The Big Bang and cosmic history
basics: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago in a hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling since. Atoms formed after about 380,000 years, stars after roughly 100 million years.
deeper: Big Bang nucleosynthesis made helium and deuterium in the first few minutes. Dark energy now accelerates the expansion.
expert: Age 13.80 Gyr; t_BBN≈3 min at T≈10⁹ K; recombination z≈1100, 380 kyr; first stars z≈20–30; ΛCDM Ω_Λ≈0.69, Ω_m≈0.31.
regime: Extrapolation back before BBN relies on theory; t<10⁻⁴³ s unknown.

title: Cosmic microwave background
basics: A faint glow of microwaves from all directions is the cooled light of the early universe, released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang. Its temperature is 2.725 K.
deeper: Tiny variations (one part in 100,000) seed galaxies. The pattern of the variations measures the universe's geometry and contents.
expert: T₀=2.7255 K; blackbody to 50 ppm (COBE); ΔT/T≈10⁻⁵; first acoustic peak ℓ≈220 → flat geometry; polarization detected.
regime: Primordial B-modes not detected.

title: Big Bang nucleosynthesis
basics: In the first minutes the universe was hot enough to fuse protons and neutrons into helium and traces of deuterium and lithium. Observed abundances match predictions.
deeper: The deuterium abundance fixes the density of ordinary matter. Lithium-7 is lower than predicted, an unresolved puzzle.
expert: Y_p≈0.245, D/H≈2.5×10⁻⁵, ³He/H≈10⁻⁵, ⁷Li/H≈5×10⁻¹⁰ (predicted) vs 1.6×10⁻¹⁰ observed.
regime: Well-tested for D and He.

title: Cosmic inflation
basics: A brief period of extremely rapid expansion in the first fraction of a second may explain why the universe is so flat and uniform and how structure began.
deeper: Quantum fluctuations stretched to cosmic size become the seeds of galaxies. Signs in gravitational-wave polarisation have not been detected.
expert: N≳60 e-folds; scalar spectral index n_s=0.965±0.004; tensor-to-scalar r<0.036 (95 %).
regime: Not directly confirmed; alternatives exist.

title: Dark energy and accelerating expansion
basics: Supernova observations in 1998 showed that the expansion of the universe is speeding up. A mysterious 'dark energy' making up about 68–69 % of the energy content is the leading explanation.
deeper: The simplest version is a cosmological constant, though its observed value is vastly smaller than quantum estimates. Whether it changes over time is being tested.
expert: w=P/ρc²=−1 for Λ; Ω_Λ≈0.685 (Planck 2018); ρ_Λ≈6×10⁻²⁷ kg/m³; deceleration parameter q₀=Ω_m/2−Ω_Λ≈−0.53.
regime: Λ still fits the data, but DESI DR2 with the CMB prefers evolving dark energy at about 3σ (2.8–4.2σ depending on the supernova sample); not yet conclusive.

title: Large-scale structure and the cosmic web
basics: Galaxies lie along filaments and walls surrounding huge empty voids. Gravity amplified tiny early fluctuations over billions of years.
deeper: Baryon acoustic oscillations leave a standard ruler of ≈147 Mpc (comoving) in galaxy clustering, used to measure expansion.
expert: BAO scale ≈147 Mpc; σ₈≈0.81; homogeneity scale ≈100 Mpc.
regime: N-body simulations match observations on large scales.

title: First stars and reionisation
basics: Models predict that the first stars lit up about 100–200 million years after the Big Bang. They have not yet been observed directly. Their ultraviolet light gradually split the neutral gas between galaxies into ions. By about a billion years the universe was largely reionised.
deeper: JWST now sees galaxies from within the first few hundred million years.
expert: Reionisation midpoint z≈7.7±0.7; optical depth τ≈0.054; first stars z≈20–30.
regime: Sources of reionisation still debated.

frontier.text: When did the first stars form, and what were they like (they have not been observed directly)?

title: Fate of the universe and the multiverse
basics: If dark energy stays constant, the universe will keep expanding forever, growing cold and dark. Ideas about other universes (multiverse) are speculative and untested.
deeper: Fine-tuning arguments ask why constants allow life; anthropic and multiverse answers are not testable so far.
expert: de Sitter (cosmic event) horizon ≈5 Gpc proper (≈16 Gly); Hawking decay of BHs ≈10⁶⁷–10¹⁰⁰ yr; Λ-dominated ⇒ a∝e^{Ht}.
regime: Speculative extrapolation. Certainty by part: heat death or Big Freeze under constant dark energy is C2; the multiverse is C4.

frontier.text: Multiverse is not testable at present

title: The observable universe
basics: We can only see as far as light has had time to reach us. The observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across and contains hundreds of billions to a couple of trillion galaxies (estimates differ).
deeper: Beyond is unseen but probably similar. Because space expands, the edge is farther than 13.8 billion light-years.
expert: Comoving radius ≈14.26 Gpc (46.5 Gly); ≈2×10¹¹ to 2×10¹² galaxies (estimates differ; Lauer et al. 2021 favour the low end); ≈10⁸⁰ baryons.
regime: Galaxy count estimates uncertain.

title: Telescopes and astronomical instruments
basics: Telescopes gather light to see faint, distant things; radio dishes, X-ray satellites and gravitational-wave detectors let us observe the universe through other channels.
deeper: Resolution is limited by diffraction, so bigger mirrors and interferometers see finer detail.
expert: θ≈1.22λ/D; JWST D=6.5 m; EHT baseline ≈ Earth diameter gives ≈20 μas at 1.3 mm; LIGO arms 4 km.
regime: Atmosphere blurs ground-based optical views.

title: The scientific method and certainty
basics: Science builds models, tests their predictions, and revises them when they fail. Confidence grows with independent tests, and no theory is ever proven final.
deeper: A good theory is falsifiable and has a stated domain of validity. Measurements are separated from interpretations of them.
expert: Bayes: P(H|D)∝P(D|H)P(H); 5σ (p≈3×10⁻⁷) is the particle-physics discovery convention, other fields use p<0.05 or Bayes factors; Occam factor penalises complexity.
regime: A norm, not a single recipe; practice differs across fields.

title: Effective theories and emergence
basics: Each scale of nature has its own simplest description: you do not need quarks to do chemistry or atoms to predict the weather. Higher-level laws emerge from lower ones but are not derived in practice.
deeper: Renormalisation explains why details at tiny scales wash out. Zooming in means switching to the deeper theory when the shallower one breaks down.
expert: RG flow dg/dlnμ=β(g); irrelevant couplings shrink as μ^(−n), so low-energy physics depends on few parameters; universality classes; weak emergence vs strong emergence.
regime: Principle, valid across physics; claims of strong emergence are contested.

title: The arrow of time
basics: The microscopic laws that govern most everyday dynamics work the same forwards and backwards (rare weak-force decays are a tiny exception that does not set the arrow), yet eggs do not unscramble. The direction of time comes from entropy increasing from a low-entropy past.
deeper: Why the early universe began with such low entropy is not explained.
expert: S=k_B ln Ω; Poincaré recurrence ∼e^{S}; ΔS_universe≥0.
regime: Statistical arrow is solid; its cosmological origin is open.

title: Information theory
basics: Information is measured in bits, as the reduction in uncertainty. Shannon showed how much data a noisy channel can carry and how far data can be compressed.
deeper: Entropy sets the best possible compression, and channel capacity sets the highest reliable data rate, and both are achievable with clever coding.
expert: H=−Σp log₂p; C=B log₂(1+S/N) for a band-limited channel with additive white Gaussian noise; mutual information I(X;Y)=H(X)−H(X|Y).
regime: Exact for stationary sources; semantic meaning not captured.

title: Landauer's principle: information is physical
basics: Erasing one bit of information must release at least a tiny amount of heat. This links information, entropy and thermodynamics.
deeper: At room temperature the minimum is about 3×10⁻²¹ joules per bit, far below what real chips dissipate.
expert: E_min=k_BT ln2=2.87×10⁻²¹ J at 300 K.
regime: Experimentally verified in small systems.
evidence: Bérut et al., Nature 483, 187 (2012): measured erasure heat in a colloidal bit

title: Computation and complexity
basics: Computers manipulate symbols by rules. Turing showed some questions (like the halting problem) cannot be decided by any program.
deeper: Complexity classes sort problems by how time grows with size. Whether P equals NP is unknown.
expert: Church-Turing thesis; halting undecidable; P⊆NP⊆PSPACE; BQP quantum polynomial time.
regime: Abstract models; physical computers are finite.

title: P versus NP
basics: If solutions to a problem can be checked fast, can they also be found fast? Most experts think not, but no one has proved it.
deeper: An answer would affect cryptography, optimisation and the limits of what any simulation can compute.
expert: P=NP? ; NP-complete: SAT, travelling salesman; best known algorithms exp-time worst case.
regime: Open problem.

title: Quantum computing
basics: Quantum computers use superposition and entanglement to tackle certain problems faster, such as factoring large numbers. Errors are the main obstacle.
deeper: Quantum error correction spreads one logical qubit over many physical qubits; useful machines need extremely low error rates.
expert: Shor: O((log N)³); Grover √N speed-up; error-correction threshold ≈10⁻²–10⁻³ for the surface code (model-dependent); best two-qubit gate errors ≈10⁻³; Google's 2024 Willow experiment showed logical error falling as the code distance grew.
regime: No large fault-tolerant machine yet.

frontier.text: Scalable fault-tolerant machines not yet built

title: Digital logic and the CPU
basics: Transistors act as switches that implement logic gates; combining billions of them builds memory and processors that run programs.
deeper: Clock speeds near 3–5 GHz are limited by heat. Moore's law (doubling of transistors) has slowed.
expert: CMOS dynamic power P=αCV²f; Boolean algebra; gate delay ≈10–20 ps; 10¹⁰–10¹¹ transistors per chip.
regime: Miniaturisation approaches atomic limits.
evidence: IRDS roadmap tables (transistor density, gate delay)

title: Artificial neural networks and machine learning
basics: Neural networks learn patterns by adjusting millions or billions of numerical weights to reduce errors on training data. They power image recognition, translation and language models.
deeper: Transformers, introduced in 2017, use attention to weigh relationships between parts of the input. Performance often improves smoothly with more data, parameters and compute.
expert: θ←θ−η∇L (SGD); backpropagation via chain rule; attention softmax(QKᵀ/√d)V; empirical scaling fits for language-model loss: L∝N^{−α_N}, α_N≈0.076 (parameters) and α_D≈0.095 (data) in Kaplan et al. 2020; Hoffmann et al. 2022 refit with a different split and optimal data about equal to parameters. These are fits, not laws.
regime: Why they generalise and how to verify their outputs are active research questions.

title: Complexity, self-organisation and networks
basics: Many interacting parts can form patterns no part intends: flocks, traffic jams, ant colonies and ecosystems. Networks with hubs or small-world links appear throughout biology and society.
deeper: Criticality, power laws and feedback loops are recurring ideas, but there is no single theory of complexity.
expert: Turing patterns: at onset the critical wavenumber is k_c²=√(det J/(D_u D_v)), so λ_c=2π/k_c=2π(D_u D_v/det J)^{1/4}; power law P(x)∼x^{−α}; the Watts-Strogatz small-world path length scales as L∼ln N.
regime: Descriptive rather than predictive in many cases.

frontier.text: Early-warning signals for tipping points are contested

title: Evolution as an information-accumulating process
basics: One useful way to describe natural selection is as a process that accumulates information about the environment in genomes, which researchers also copy in evolutionary algorithms.
deeper: Selection works with variation, inheritance and differential success at any scale from RNA molecules to ecosystems.
expert: Fisher's fundamental theorem: the rate of increase in mean fitness due to natural selection equals the additive genetic variance in fitness, dW̄/dt=Var_A(W) (divided by W̄ in the discrete-time form); Price equation Δz̄=Cov(w,z)/w̄+E(wΔz)/w̄.
regime: Substrate-independent principle.

frontier.text: How should the information that selection puts into genomes be defined and measured?

title: Scaling laws and dimensional analysis
basics: Many natural features change with size in predictable ways: a mouse and an elephant differ in metabolism, strength and cooling. Dimensional analysis finds such relations from units alone. Across animals, resting metabolic rate rises roughly as mass to the power 2/3 to 3/4 (Kleiber's 3/4 is the usual fit; the exponent and its explanation are debated).
deeper: Metabolic rate scales as mass to the power of about three quarters across animals, while strength and heat loss follow area versus volume.
expert: Kleiber B∝M^{3/4}; square-cube: area∝L², volume∝L³; Reynolds, Froude numbers dimensionless.
regime: Exponents debated for some taxa.

frontier.text: Is metabolic scaling a single power law, and what sets the exponent?

title: Units, constants and measurement
basics: Since 2019 all SI units are defined by fixing exact values of fundamental constants such as the speed of light, Planck's constant and the elementary charge.
deeper: This makes the kilogram depend on h, not a metal cylinder. Measurements always carry uncertainties that must be quoted.
regime: Definitions are exact by convention.

title: Power grid and transformers
basics: Generators spin magnets inside coils, producing AC electricity. Transformers raise the voltage for long-distance lines to cut heat losses, then lower it for homes.
deeper: Power loss goes as current squared times resistance, so transmitting at high voltage means lower current. The grid must balance supply and demand every instant.
expert: P_loss=I²R=(P/V)²R; transmission 110–765 kV; mains 50/60 Hz; 3-phase P=√3 V I cosφ.
regime: Storage and renewable variability drive grid research.

title: Electric motors
basics: A current-carrying coil in a magnetic field feels a force and turns. Motors are generators run in reverse, and motor-driven systems account for roughly 45–55 % of global electricity use (IEA estimates).
deeper: Efficiency of large motors exceeds 95 %.
expert: τ=NIAB sinθ; back-EMF ε=kΦω; P=τω.
regime: Heat and magnet materials limit power density.

title: Batteries
basics: A battery stores energy in chemical form and releases it as electric current when ions and electrons move between electrodes. Lithium-ion cells shuttle lithium ions in and out of layered materials.
deeper: Energy density of Li-ion is about 250 Wh/kg, far less than gasoline per mass. Solid-state batteries aim to improve safety and density.
expert: E=∫V dQ≈Q·V_avg (Wh = Ah × V; a capacitor stores ½CV² and its voltage falls as it discharges); Li-ion ≈150–270 Wh/kg; gasoline ≈12,000 Wh/kg; LiCoO₂ + C₆ chemistry ≈3.7 V.
regime: Degradation and dendrite growth limit lifetimes.

title: Flight
basics: Aircraft stay up because wings deflect air downward and the pressure difference gives lift. Engines provide thrust to overcome drag.
deeper: Jet engines compress, heat and expand air. Birds and insects use flapping and unsteady vortices.
expert: L=½ρv²SC_L; L/D≈15–20 airliner; Re≈10⁷; takeoff speed ≈70 m/s.
regime: Supersonic flight adds shock waves and wave drag.

title: Lasers and fibre optics
basics: Light travels along glass fibres by total internal reflection. Lasers send pulses carrying data at terabits per second across oceans.
deeper: Glass with attenuation of about 0.2 dB/km made modern internet cables possible.
expert: θ_c=arcsin(n₂/n₁); attenuation ≈0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm; capacity is bounded by the nonlinear Shannon limit, which depends on bandwidth used and fibre type; single-core fibre demonstrations now exceed 300 Tb/s over a ~37 THz band (NICT 2024: 402 Tb/s estimated, 378 Tb/s decoded, 50 km).
regime: Nonlinear effects limit power in fibre.

title: LEDs and laser diodes
basics: In a diode, electrons and holes combine and emit light. LEDs make efficient lighting and laser diodes power barcode scanners and communications.
deeper: The colour is set by the band gap of the semiconductor.
expert: λ(nm)≈1240/E_g(eV); GaN has E_g≈3.4 eV (≈365 nm, UV); blue LEDs use InGaN quantum wells with E_g≈2.7 eV (≈460 nm); LED efficacy >150 lm/W.
regime: Efficiency drops at high current (droop).

title: Radio and wireless communication
basics: Radio sends information by modulating electromagnetic waves. Phones, Wi-Fi and satellites all use different frequency bands.
deeper: Antennas of about half a wavelength radiate efficiently. Capacity limits come from bandwidth and noise.
expert: Dipole length ≈λ/2; Friis P_r=P_tG_tG_r(λ/4πd)²; Wi-Fi 2.4/5 GHz; 5G 0.6–52 GHz.
regime: Spectrum is a limited resource.

title: Fusion power research
basics: Fusion could provide energy from hydrogen isotopes, but holding plasma hotter than the Sun's core is hard. In 2022 a laser shot at the NIF produced more fusion energy than the laser delivered to the target, but not a power plant.
deeper: Tokamaks use magnetic confinement; NIF uses lasers to compress fuel pellets.
expert: Lawson: nTτ≳3×10²¹ keV s m⁻³; D-T 150 million K; NIF target gain ≈1.5 in Dec 2022 (3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ) and a record 4.13 in Apr 2025 (8.6 MJ from 2.08 MJ); the lasers draw about 300 MJ from the grid per shot, so the whole system is far from net energy.
regime: No net-power reactor yet.

title: Plasma: the fourth state of matter
basics: A plasma is a gas hot enough that atoms lose electrons. Stars, lightning and auroras are plasma, which makes up most visible matter in the universe.
deeper: Plasmas respond collectively to electric and magnetic fields. They carry currents and support waves.
expert: Debye length λ_D=√(ε₀kT/ne²); plasma frequency ω_p=√(ne²/ε₀m); ionisation at ≳10⁴ K.
regime: Collective behaviour requires many particles within a Debye sphere (nλ_D³≫1) and system size ≫λ_D.

title: 3D printing (additive manufacturing)
basics: A 3D printer builds objects layer by layer from a digital model by depositing, melting or curing material. It allows shapes hard to make by cutting.
deeper: Metals can be printed by melting powder with lasers; resolution is tens of micrometres.
expert: Layer thickness 20–200 μm; laser PBF melt-pool ≈100 μm; build rates ≈10–100 cm³/h.
regime: Part strength depends on process defects.

title: Supply, demand and choice
basics: Prices tend to settle where the amount buyers want equals what sellers offer. Scarcity forces choices and every choice has an opportunity cost.
deeper: Comparative advantage shows why trade benefits both sides even when one is better at everything. Externalities and public goods are cases where markets alone misallocate.
expert: Q_d=a−bP, Q_s=c+dP, P*=(a−c)/(b+d); elasticity ε=(dQ/Q)/(dP/P); consumer+producer surplus.
regime: Assumes rational agents and competition; real markets have frictions.
