frontier.text: How well do simple rational-agent models predict real economic behaviour?

title: Game theory and cooperation
basics: Game theory analyses strategic choices where each outcome depends on others. The prisoner's dilemma shows why self-interest can defeat cooperation, and repeated play can restore it.
deeper: Evolutionary game theory applies the same logic to animals and microbes, showing how cooperation can evolve.
expert: Nash equilibrium: no profitable unilateral deviation; PD payoffs T>R>P>S; replicator dynamics ẋ=x(f−f̄).
regime: Human behaviour deviates from rational-actor models.

frontier.text: How often do people and organisations settle on equilibrium play in real strategic situations?

title: Growth, inflation and money
basics: Economies are measured by output (GDP), prices and jobs. Central banks adjust interest rates to steer inflation and employment.
deeper: Long-run growth follows capital, labour and technology. How much policy affects growth, inequality and recessions is debated.
expert: GDP=C+I+G+(X−M); π=ΔP/P; Solow Y=K^αL^{1−α}; Taylor rule i=r*+π+0.5(π−π*)+0.5y.
regime: Macro causation debated; models are policy-dependent.

frontier.text: Causes of growth, inequality and policy effects

title: Behavioural biases and decision-making
basics: People rely on mental shortcuts that cause systematic errors, such as loss aversion and anchoring. Incentives and defaults change behaviour strongly.
deeper: Prospect theory describes how losses weigh more than gains. Many classic effects replicate; others do not.
expert: Value v(x)=x^α (x≥0), −λ(−x)^β (x<0), λ≈2.25; hyperbolic discounting V=A/(1+kD).
regime: Effect sizes vary with context.

frontier.text: How large and general is loss aversion, and how robust are default and nudge effects outside the original studies?

title: Society, culture and institutions
basics: Sociology studies how groups, norms, institutions and inequality shape behaviour. Methods include surveys, ethnography and experiments.
deeper: Social structures such as family, education, work and government emerge from many interactions and persist over generations.
expert: Gini coefficient G∈[0,1]; social network homophily; Dunbar's number (≈150 for typical human network size) is a contested estimate: a 2021 reanalysis found the statistical basis cannot support a single figure (95 % CI ≈4–520).
regime: Findings are context-dependent, causal claims are harder.

frontier.text: How much of social behaviour can be explained by individual choice versus social structure?

title: Human development across the lifespan
basics: People develop physically, cognitively and socially from infancy through old age. Early experience, genes and environment all contribute.
deeper: Piaget and Vygotsky proposed stages and social learning. Attachment in infancy shapes later relationships.
expert: Brain ≈350 g at birth →1,300 g at 6 yr; peak bone mass ≈ age 30; life expectancy ≈73 yr global.
regime: Stage theories are approximate.

frontier.text: How do genes, environment and chance combine to shape development across a lifetime?

title: Language and communication
basics: Language is a learned symbolic system humans use to share thoughts. Children acquire it rapidly and speakers invent new sentences constantly.
deeper: Language relies on a distributed left-lateralised network that includes, but is not limited to, Broca's and Wernicke's areas. About 7,000 languages exist, and many are endangered.
expert: ≈7,000 living languages; a six-year-old's vocabulary is estimated at roughly 5,000–14,000 words depending on how a "word" is counted; Zipf f∝1/rank.
regime: Debates over innate grammar versus learning.

frontier.text: How much of grammar is innate, and how much is learned from experience?

title: Evidence-based medicine and epidemiology
basics: Randomised controlled trials and epidemiology tell which treatments work and what causes disease. Confidence rises with replication and consistent mechanisms.
deeper: Confounding and bias can mislead observational studies, so randomisation and blinding are the reference methods.
expert: Relative risk RR=I_exp/I_unexp; NNT=1/ARR; p-value; R₀ and herd immunity threshold 1−1/R₀ (homogeneous mixing, fully effective vaccine).
regime: Subject to ethical and practical limits.

title: Number theory and cryptography
basics: Prime numbers and modular arithmetic underlie secure communication. Public-key cryptography relies on problems like factoring large numbers being hard.
deeper: RSA uses the product of two large primes; a large quantum computer running Shor's algorithm would break it, motivating new schemes.
expert: RSA: c=m^e mod N, N=pq; Euler φ(N)=(p−1)(q−1); prime density π(x)≈x/ln x.
regime: Security rests on unproven hardness assumptions.

title: Geometry, topology and fractals
basics: Geometry studies shapes and distances; topology studies properties unchanged by stretching, like holes. Fractals are shapes that look similar at every scale, such as coastlines and ferns.
deeper: Topology classifies phases of matter and knots in DNA. Fractal dimension quantifies roughness.
expert: Euler characteristic χ=V−E+F=2−2g; similarity dimension D=ln N/ln(1/s) (equals the Hausdorff dimension for the Koch curve, 1.26); Mandelbrot set.
regime: Idealised mathematical objects.

title: Regression, modelling and data
basics: Statistical models fit curves to data to estimate relationships and make predictions. Correlation does not by itself show cause.
deeper: Least squares finds the line minimising squared errors. Overfitting happens when a model fits noise.
expert: ŷ=β₀+β₁x; β₁=Cov(x,y)/Var(x); R²=1−SS_res/SS_tot; AIC=2k−2 ln L̂.
regime: Assumes linearity and independent errors.

title: The photon and light quanta
basics: A photon is a single quantum of electromagnetic radiation, massless and travelling at light speed. Detectors register light as individual clicks.
deeper: Photons carry momentum p=h/λ, enabling radiation pressure and solar sails. Their spin is 1, giving two polarisations.
expert: E=hf=pc; m_γ<10⁻¹⁸ eV (limit); full sun: ≈1.2×10²¹ photons/(m² s) in 400–700 nm (≈2000 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹ at peak summer noon).
regime: Wave model suffices when many photons.

title: Equivalence principle and gravity tests
basics: All objects fall the same way in a gravitational field, so locally gravity feels the same as acceleration. This idea led Einstein to general relativity.
deeper: Torsion balances test it to about 1 part in 10¹³ and the MICROSCOPE satellite to a few parts in 10¹⁵.
expert: η=2|a₁−a₂|/(a₁+a₂); MICROSCOPE final result η(Ti,Pt)=(−1.5±2.3(stat)±1.5(syst))×10⁻¹⁵ (1σ), consistent with zero; gravitational redshift Δf/f=gh/c².
regime: Tested to about 10⁻¹⁵ for ordinary matter; antihydrogen has been shown to fall downward (ALPHA-g, 2023) but only at the tens-of-percent level.

title: Quark-gluon plasma
basics: At temperatures above ~2 trillion kelvin, quarks and gluons are no longer confined and behave as a hot fluid like the universe a microsecond after the Big Bang.
deeper: Heavy-ion collisions at RHIC and the LHC create tiny droplets that flow with very low viscosity.
expert: Crossover temperature T_pc≈156 MeV≈1.8×10¹² K (no sharp T_c at zero baryon density); critical energy density about 0.3–0.5 GeV/fm³ (lattice); η/s within a small factor of the conjectured 1/4π bound.
regime: Created only briefly in colliders.

frontier.text: Is there a critical point in the QCD phase diagram?

title: Superfluids and Bose-Einstein condensates
basics: At very low temperature, helium-4 flows without friction and atomic clouds can collapse into a single quantum state. Quantum effects become visible on large scales.
deeper: Bosons can all occupy the same state; fermion pairs can do the same, as in superconductors.
expert: BEC T_c=(2πħ²/mk_B)(n/ζ(3/2))^{2/3}; ⁴He λ-point 2.17 K; BEC achieved 1995 at ≈170 nK.
regime: Needs cooling near absolute zero.

title: Solar wind, magnetosphere and aurora
basics: The Sun blows a stream of charged particles (solar wind) past Earth. Earth's magnetic field deflects most of it. Energy from the wind is stored in the magnetotail, and when it is released it accelerates electrons down the field lines into the upper atmosphere near the poles, where they excite oxygen and nitrogen to glow as aurora.
deeper: Solar storms can disturb satellites, radio and power grids. The heliosphere shields the solar system from some galactic cosmic rays.
expert: Wind speed 300–800 km/s, n≈5 cm⁻³; heliopause ≈120 AU; Dst index −100 to −500 nT in storms.
regime: Forecasting flare and CME arrival is imprecise.

title: Mars
basics: Mars is a cold, dry world with a thin carbon-dioxide atmosphere, but ancient river valleys and minerals show it once had liquid water.
deeper: Its surface holds the Solar System's tallest volcano, Olympus Mons. Rovers search for signs of past life.
expert: R=3390 km; g=3.71 m/s²; surface P≈600 Pa; T≈210 K; Olympus Mons ≈22 km high; sidereal rotation 24.62 h, solar day (sol) 24.66 h.
regime: Whether Mars hosted life is unknown.

title: Venus and runaway greenhouse
basics: Venus is similar in size to Earth but has a 92-bar carbon-dioxide atmosphere that holds the surface near 460 °C. It is a warning of an extreme greenhouse effect.
deeper: Its clouds of sulfuric acid hide the surface; it rotates backwards very slowly (243 Earth days, sidereal). A runaway greenhouse is the leading explanation for the loss of its water, not a measured history.
expert: T_s≈737 K, P≈92 bar, albedo ≈0.76 (so T_eff≈230 K), greenhouse warming ≈500 K.
regime: Past water history uncertain.

frontier.text: Past oceans and habitability of Venus

title: Jupiter, Saturn and the giant planets
basics: Jupiter and Saturn are mostly hydrogen and helium with deep layers of metallic hydrogen, banded clouds and strong winds. Jupiter's mass is 318 Earths.
deeper: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a centuries-old storm. Uranus and Neptune have more ices and are tilted or windy.
expert: M_J=1.898×10²⁷ kg=318 M_E; R_J=69 911 km; Saturn density 0.69 g/cm³; Jupiter's fastest jet ≈140–150 m/s (≈500–540 km/h; JWST ≈515 km/h); Saturn's equatorial jet ≈400–500 m/s (≈1,400–1,800 km/h); Neptune ≈580 m/s (≈2,100 km/h, Voyager 2).
regime: Interior structure inferred from gravity data.

title: Pluto and the Kuiper belt
basics: Pluto is a small icy world with mountains of water ice, nitrogen glaciers and a big moon, Charon. It belongs to a belt of icy bodies beyond Neptune.
deeper: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 because it has not cleared its orbit.
expert: R=1188 km; a=39.5 AU; P=248 yr; e=0.25; N₂ glaciers; Charon/Pluto mass ratio ≈0.12.
regime: Classification is a convention.

title: Earth as a planet
basics: Earth is the only known planet with liquid-water oceans, plate tectonics and life. Its size, distance and magnetic field help keep it habitable.
deeper: The Moon damps the tilt's wobble; without it the tilt would vary faster over a wider range, but simulations disagree on how large and how harmful the change would be. Earth's interior heat comes from primordial energy and radioactive decay.
expert: M=5.972×10²⁴ kg; R=6371 km; g=9.81 m/s²; a=1 AU; day 23.93 h; axial tilt 23.44°; surface heat flow ≈47 TW.
regime: Properties precisely measured.

title: Plants: water transport and growth
basics: Plants pull water from roots to leaves through narrow tubes (xylem), using evaporation from leaves as the pump. Sugars made in leaves are moved to roots and fruit through phloem.
deeper: Pores called stomata open to let CO₂ in and water out. Hormones such as auxin steer growth toward light.
expert: Cohesion-tension: leaf water potential ≈−1 to −3 MPa (a gradient of about −0.01 to −0.02 MPa per metre of height); tall trees >100 m; transpiration ≈99 % of water absorbed; open stomatal aperture ≈3–10 μm wide, guard-cell pair 10–30 μm long.
regime: Limits tree height ≈130 m.

title: Flowers, pollinators and seed dispersal
basics: Flowers advertise to insects and birds with colour and scent, and the animals carry pollen between plants. About 75 % of food crops benefit from animal pollination.
deeper: Bees see ultraviolet and see patterns we cannot. Co-evolution has produced matched shapes, like long tongues and tubular flowers.
expert: ≈90 % of flowering plants animal-pollinated; honey bee flies ≈6.7 m/s, wingbeat ≈230 Hz; 35 % of crop production volume depends on pollinators.
regime: Pollinator declines are documented in places.

frontier.text: How large are pollinator declines, and how much do they reduce crop and wild-plant yields?

title: Animal diversity and fungi
basics: Animals range from sponges to mammals; most species are insects. Fungi are neither plants nor animals and decompose and partner with plant roots.
deeper: Vertebrates have backbones; arthropods have jointed legs and exoskeletons. Fungal networks (mycelium) can span hectares.
expert: ≈1 M described insect species; ≈66 000 vertebrate; ≈150 000 fungi described; blue whale ≈150 t.
regime: Classification updated by genomics.

title: Tsunamis and natural hazards
basics: Undersea earthquakes can displace the ocean floor and launch tsunamis that cross ocean basins at jet speed. Landslides, floods and volcanic eruptions are other major hazards.
deeper: In deep water a tsunami is a long, low wave; near shore it slows and grows tall.
expert: v=√(gh); h=4000 m → v≈200 m/s (≈720 km/h); wavelength ≈100–200 km; Green's law A∝h^{−1/4}.
regime: v=√(gh) and Green's law apply to a linear, long wave (wavelength much greater than depth) over slowly varying depth; near shore, nonlinearity, breaking and run-up dominate and need full models. Warning systems rely on seismic and ocean sensors.

title: El Niño and the Southern Oscillation
basics: Every few years the tropical Pacific alternates between warm (El Niño) and cool (La Niña) phases, shifting rain and storms worldwide.
deeper: It arises from coupled ocean-atmosphere feedback. Forecasts a few months ahead have useful skill.
expert: Period ≈2–7 yr; Niño-3.4 SST anomaly ±0.5 °C threshold; Bjerknes feedback.
regime: Effects of warming on ENSO behaviour are debated.

title: Biomes and climate zones
basics: Temperature and rainfall decide whether a region becomes rainforest, desert, grassland or tundra. Biomes are broad ecosystem types shaped by climate.
deeper: Mountain height, ocean currents and latitude shift these patterns. Plant form and animal life match the local climate.
expert: Whittaker diagram: precipitation vs mean temperature; tropical forest >2000 mm/yr, desert <250 mm/yr.
regime: Biome boundaries shift with climate.

title: Fossils and palaeontology
basics: Fossils are preserved traces of ancient life in rock. They show how life changed and when groups appeared.
deeper: Rare conditions are needed: fast burial and mineralisation. The record is incomplete but shows many transitional forms.
expert: Oldest widely accepted traces of life ≈3.4–3.5 Ga (stromatolites and microfossils; interpretation of the oldest ones is disputed), with older claims up to ≥3.7 Ga contested; Cambrian starts ≈538.8 Ma; Tiktaalik ≈375 Ma; Archaeopteryx ≈150 Ma.
regime: Preservation bias skews the record.

title: Energy sources and use
basics: Humanity runs mostly on fossil fuels, with growing shares from hydro, nuclear, wind and solar. All sources must obey energy conservation and the second law.
deeper: Energy density, cost and emissions differ widely. Electricity is flexible but must be generated and used at the same moment unless stored.
expert: World primary energy ≈6×10²⁰ J/yr (≈19 TW); solar flux at ground ≈170 W/m² average; coal ≈24 MJ/kg; wind turbine Betz limit 59.3 %.
regime: Mix and costs change over years.

title: Population and agriculture
basics: Human population is about eight billion, fed largely thanks to the Green Revolution, synthetic fertiliser and irrigation. Growth is slowing as fertility falls.
deeper: Agriculture uses about half of habitable land and large amounts of fresh water, and drives habitat loss and emissions.
expert: Doubling time=ln2/r; total fertility rate replacement ≈2.1; agriculture (cropland plus pasture) uses about half of the world's habitable land (about 38 % of ice-free land, FAO).
regime: Projections depend on assumptions about fertility.

frontier.text: When will world population peak, and at what level (UN and IHME projections differ)?

title: Conservation laws as a unifying thread
basics: Energy, momentum, angular momentum and electric charge follow from symmetries and have never been seen violated. Baryon number is conserved in all observed processes (proton lifetime >10³⁴ yr), but it is only an accidental symmetry: the Standard Model violates it non-perturbatively (sphalerons, conserving B−L), and the universe's matter excess requires some violation. Conservation laws let us predict outcomes without knowing the details of an interaction.
deeper: Each is tested to extraordinary precision; any claimed violation would revolutionise physics.
expert: Proton lifetime >10³⁴ yr (baryon number); charge conservation: e⁻ lifetime >6.6×10²⁸ yr.
regime: Energy conservation is subtle in cosmology.

title: String theory and holography
basics: String theory replaces point particles with tiny vibrating strings and naturally includes gravity. It has inspired deep mathematics but has made no tested prediction yet.
deeper: Holography (AdS/CFT) links a gravity theory in one space to a quantum theory without gravity on its boundary. It works for a universe with negative cosmological constant, unlike ours; a de Sitter version is not established. It is a useful model of quantum gravity, not a description of our universe. The theory allows an enormous "landscape" of possible universes.
expert: String length ℓ_s≈ℓ_P; critical dimension 10 (superstring) or 11 (M-theory); AdS/CFT: Z_gravity=Z_CFT; landscape ≳10⁵⁰⁰ vacua (estimate).
regime: Mathematically rich; no experimental support; no supersymmetric partners found at the LHC.

title: Loop quantum gravity and other approaches
basics: Loop quantum gravity treats space as made of tiny discrete units. Asymptotic safety and causal sets are other attempts to quantise gravity without strings.
deeper: These programmes try to remove the singularities of black holes and the Big Bang.
expert: Area spectrum A=8πγℓ_P²Σ√(j(j+1)); the Barbero-Immirzi parameter γ is free; matching the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy fixes it to ≈0.127 or ≈0.24 depending on how the horizon states are counted.
regime: Not tested.

title: Could machines be conscious?
basics: There is no agreed test for whether an artificial system could have experience. Different theories of consciousness give different answers, and the status of integrated information theory is itself disputed (open letter, 2023). Theories of consciousness are C3; machine consciousness is C4.
deeper: Behaviour alone may not settle it, because systems trained on human text can talk about experience without having any.
expert: IIT: Φ depends on physical causal structure, not on software; functionalist theories: organisation suffices.
regime: Speculative; depends on unsettled theory of consciousness.
